metadata.scope: e_rajastan (398 baronies across k_delhi, k_gujarat, k_himalaya, k_kashmir, k_kosala, k_malwa, k_punjab, k_rajputana, k_sindh)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_asigarh.first_mention_attestation: Epigraphically attested as the fort of Asika (Asigarh) in the 1168 CE Hansi stone inscription of Chahamana ruler Prithviraja II; earlier Ghaznavid chronicles (such as Baihaqi's Tarikh-i-Mas'udi) record the fortress town of Hansi during Mas'ud I's 1037 CE siege.
b_asigarh.etymology_analysis: Compound of Sanskrit asi ('sword') and Hindi/Prakrit garh ('fort'), literally 'Fort of Swords', the historic medieval fortress at Hansi in Hisar district, Haryana (epigraphically Asika).

b_asika.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ashika (Asika) in the 1170 CE Bijolia rock inscription of Chahamana ruler Someshvara, recording Vigraharaja IV's capture of Dhillika and Ashika (modern Hansi / Asigarh Fort, which also yielded 7th–8th century CE Gupta/post-Gupta Jain bronzes).
b_asika.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Asika (also Asidurga/Asigarh), from asi ('sword'), reflecting its medieval reputation as a sword-making center; later vernacularized as Hansi.

b_narabhata.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical or epigraphic sources; appears as a medieval/local place-name variant in Haryana (distinct from Narnaul).
b_narabhata.etymology_analysis: Compound of Sanskrit nara ('man/hero') and bhata ('warrior/soldier'), used as a regional settlement name.

b_sarasvati.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sarasvati in the Rigveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE) as a sacred river in northwestern India; the regional town of Sirsa (ancient Sairishaka) is also linked to the river in local tradition.
b_sarasvati.etymology_analysis: Directly adopts the Vedic hydronym Sarasvati (Sanskrit saras + -vati, 'she who possesses pools/waters'), referring to the ancient sacred river of Haryana/Rajasthan.

b_bhatnir.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval chronicles in connection with Bhatiya / Bhatner around 1004 CE during Mahmud of Ghazni's campaign; later renamed Hanumangarh in 1805 CE by Raja Surat Singh of Bikaner.
b_bhatnir.etymology_analysis: Bhatner/Bhatnir means 'fortress of the Bhatis', combining the Bhati Rajput clan name with -ner ('fortress/town').

b_tribandapura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the exact form Tribandapura in pre-867 CE historical sources (used as a Sanskritized placeholder for the Bathinda/Tabarhind region in Punjab).
b_tribandapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized compound of tri ('three'), bandha ('bond/dam/fortification'), and pura ('city/town').

b_sunam.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval Persian chronicles of the Ghurid/Delhi Sultanate period (late 12th–13th century CE, such as Tabaqat-i-Nasiri) as an important iqta in Punjab.
b_sunam.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Sanskrit Sunama ('of good name/auspicious fame'), associated with the ancient Suraj Kund sun temple site near the town.

b_jajjanir.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Jajjanir (Jajner/Janer) in Al-Biruni's Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030 CE) as a town on the route in Punjab.
b_jajjanir.etymology_analysis: Medieval Punjabi toponym recorded in Perso-Arabic sources as Jajjanir (modern Janer), likely combining a personal or clan name with -nir ('settlement/stronghold').

b_indraprastha.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Indraprastha in the Mahabharata and as Indapatta in the Pali Buddhist canon (c. 5th–3rd century BCE) as the ancient capital of the Kuru kingdom on the Yamuna (identified with Purana Qila in Delhi).
b_indraprastha.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Indraprastha ('Plain of Indra' or 'City of Indra'), the ancient Kuru capital on the Yamuna river attested centuries BCE in Sanskrit epic and Pali Buddhist literature.

b_dhilika.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dhillika in the 1170 CE Bijolia rock inscription of Chahamana king Someshvara.
b_dhilika.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized form Dhillika of the early medieval settlement name Dhilli (modern Delhi).

b_jahanpanah.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1326–1327 CE by Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq as the fourth medieval city of Delhi.
b_jahanpanah.etymology_analysis: Persian compound Jahan-panah ('Refuge of the World'), named by Muhammad bin Tughluq in 1326–1327 CE.

b_rohtak.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Rohitaka in ancient Sanskrit and Buddhist texts (Mahabharata, Divyavadana) and associated with Yaudheya coinage (2nd century BCE–4th century CE).
b_rohtak.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Rohitaka ('place abounding in Rohida/red trees' or associated with the Mattamayuraka Yaudheyas).

b_hastinapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hastinapura (Pali Hatthinipura) in the Mahabharata and early Buddhist literature (c. 5th–3rd century BCE) as the capital of the Kuru kingdom.
b_hastinapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Hastinapura ('City of Elephants' or city of King Hastin), from hastin ('elephant') and pura ('city').

b_mirath.first_mention_attestation: While the site features a 3rd-century BCE Ashokan pillar, the medieval name Mirath (modern Meerut) is attested from the 11th century CE onward (e.g., Ghaznavid-era accounts; traditional etymology links it to Mayarashtra).
b_mirath.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Sanskrit Mayarashtra ('Kingdom of Maya'), evolving through Prakrit into Mirath/Meerut.

b_indrasthana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a distinct historical city name in pre-867 CE sources (a variant/Sanskritization of Indraprastha).
b_indrasthana.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound of Indra (Vedic deity) and sthana ('place/abode'), parallel to Indraprastha.

b_hapur.first_mention_attestation: According to local historical tradition, founded around 983 CE as Haripur by Haradatta, the Dor Rajput chieftain of Bulandshahr and Meerut.
b_hapur.eponym_details: Named Haripur (later contracted to Hapur) after Haradatta, the Dor chieftain who founded it c. 983 CE.
b_hapur.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Haripur ('City of Hari / Haradatta'), founded c. 983 CE.

b_saharanpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1340 CE during the reign of Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, who named the town Shah-Harunpur (later contracted to Saharanpur) in honor of the Chishti Sufi saint Shah Harun Chishti.
b_saharanpur.eponym_details: Named Shah-Harunpur (contracted to Saharanpur) after the 14th-century Sufi saint Shah Harun Chishti during Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq's c. 1340 CE campaign.

morphemes.translation: personal name of Sufi saint Shah Harun Chishti

b_saharanpur.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Shah-Harunpur ('City of Shah Harun'), combining the personal name of the 14th-century Chishti saint Shah Harun with the Indo-Aryan settlement suffix -pur.

b_sthanisvara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sthanvishvara / Sthanisvara in Banabhatta's Harshacharita (early 7th century CE) and visited by Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang c. 635 CE (as Sa-ta-ni-shi-fa-lo).
b_sthanisvara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Sthanvishvara / Sthanisvara ('Lord of the Place' or 'Abode of Shiva Sthanu-Ishvara'), capital of the Pushyabhuti dynasty and modern Thanesar in Haryana.

b_sirhind.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Persian chronicles from the late 12th century CE onward (often associated with Tabarhind/Sirhind as the frontier fortress of Hind).
b_sirhind.etymology_analysis: Popularly interpreted from Persian Sar-i-Hind ('Frontier/Head of India'), though some scholars also link it to the ancient Sairindhra tribe.

b_samana.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Delhi Sultanate chronicles (late 12th–13th century CE) as an important administrative and military outpost in Punjab.
b_samana.etymology_analysis: Toponym in Patiala district, Punjab, attested from the early Sultanate period; local tradition links it to Imamgarh or a personal name.

b_sadhaura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; attested in medieval and Mughal-era records in Haryana.
b_sadhaura.etymology_analysis: Locally derived from Sadhuwara ('abode/settlement of sadhus'), contracted to Sadhaura.

b_kol.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval chronicles upon its conquest by Qutb al-Din Aibak in 1194 CE (and in the 1311 CE Chanderi inscription as khitta of Kol); pre-12th-century history is obscure.
b_kol.etymology_analysis: Ancient/medieval name of Aligarh, variously attributed to the Kol tribe or a local chieftain before its 18th-century renaming to Aligarh.

b_soron.first_mention_attestation: Known as Sukarakshetra in the Varaha Purana; the earliest extant temple remains (Sita-Ram temple) date to around the 9th–10th century CE.
b_soron.etymology_analysis: Vernacular contraction of Sanskrit Sukarakshetra ('Field of the Boar'), the pilgrimage site associated with Varaha.

b_etah.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; attested in medieval/Mughal-era records in western Uttar Pradesh.
b_etah.etymology_analysis: Popularly derived from Hindi inta ('brick'), referring to a brick mound or settlement founded by Chauhan Rajputs in the medieval period.

b_mathura.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Mauryan/post-Mauryan inscriptions (c. 3rd–2nd century BCE), Buddhist texts, and later in Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd century CE) as Modoura.
b_mathura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Madhura/Mathura, traditionally associated with Madhuvana ('forest of Madhu') on the Yamuna.

b_krishnajanmabhoomi.first_mention_attestation: While Mathura is ancient, the specific compound name Krishnajanmabhoomi ('Birthplace of Krishna') for the temple complex is a later/modern designation not attested as a settlement name by 867 CE.
b_krishnajanmabhoomi.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound meaning 'Land/Site of Krishna's Birth', referring to the sacred temple complex in Mathura.

b_govardhan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Govardhana Hill in the Harivamsa (c. 3rd–4th century CE) and early Puranas, and in Kushan-era Mathura traditions.
b_govardhan.etymology_analysis: Directly adopts the oronym Govardhana (Sanskrit go + vardhana, 'nourisher of cattle'), the sacred hill near Mathura.

b_agra.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary attestation under the name Agra occurs in the Persian divan of Ghaznavid poet Mas'ud Sa'd Salman (c. 1080–1081 CE), describing Sultan Ibrahim's campaign against the fortress of Agra; later refounded as the Lodi capital in 1504 CE by Sikandar Lodi.

morphemes.translation: foremost, front; or linked to Agravana ('foremost forest') or Hindi agar ('salt-pan')

b_agra.etymology_analysis: First attested as Agra in late 11th-century Persian poetry (c. 1080 CE); traditionally linked either to the Mahabharata forest name Agravana ('foremost forest') or to Hindi agar ('salt-pan').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Mahabharata (c. 4th–3rd century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Agravana ('foremost forest') is attested in the Mahabharata as a sacred grove along the Yamuna traditionally associated with the site of modern Agra.

b_sripatha.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sripatha in the 1043 CE Bayana inscription of Jadaun king Vijayapala.
b_sripatha.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Sripatha ('Auspicious Path'), the medieval Sanskrit name of Bayana in eastern Rajasthan.

b_bayana.first_mention_attestation: Recorded epigraphically from the 11th century CE (1043 CE Bayana inscription of Vijayapala; earlier Gupta-era Vishnuvardhana pillar at Bijaigarh does not attest the name Bayana).
b_bayana.etymology_analysis: Locally linked to Banasura (Banapura -> Bayana), or evolved from Prakrit forms of the medieval town name.

b_dhavalapuri.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dhavalapuri in the Dholpur stone inscription of Chahamana ruler Chandamahasena, dated Vikrama Samvat 898 (20 April 842 CE).
b_dhavalapuri.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Dhavalapuri ('White City'), modern Dholpur in Rajasthan, attested in the 842 CE Chahamana inscription.

b_mandawar.first_mention_attestation: Attested under the name Mandawar during Timur's 1399 CE campaign across the upper Ganga plains and subsequently recorded as a pargana in the late 16th-century Ain-i-Akbari; unattested as Mandawar by 867 CE.
b_mandawar.etymology_analysis: Historic town in Bijnor district, Uttar Pradesh, identified archaeologically by Alexander Cunningham with the 7th-century city of Matipura; the vernacular name Mandawar is attested from the late medieval period.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (c. 634–635 CE, Mo-ti-pu-lo)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Matipura, visited and described by Xuanzang c. 634–635 CE, is identified by Alexander Cunningham with the old mound of Mandawar in Bijnor district.

b_bijnor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; local tradition attributes its foundation to Bijli Pasi in the medieval period.
b_bijnor.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym in western Uttar Pradesh, locally linked to King Bijli Pasi or to Sanskrit Vijaynagar.

b_gangadvara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Gangadvara ('Gate of the Ganga') in the Mahabharata and Puranas, and described as Mo-yu-lo (Mayura) near Gangadvara by Xuanzang in the 7th century CE.
b_gangadvara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound Gangadvara ('Gate of the Ganges'), the ancient name of Haridwar where the Ganges enters the North Indian plain.

b_sambhal.first_mention_attestation: First contemporarily attested in Delhi Sultanate records (c. 13th–14th century CE) after Qutb al-Din Aibak's conquest; local lore links it to Puranic Shambhala.
b_sambhal.etymology_analysis: Vernacularized from Sanskrit Shambhala, an ancient literary/mythic name applied to the medieval town of Sambhal in Rohilkhand.

b_amroha.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval chronicles by 1305 CE (Battle of Amroha under Alauddin Khalji); local tradition attributes its founding to Amba Devi or Raja Amar Singh.
b_amroha.etymology_analysis: Folk etymology derives Amroha from am ('mango') and rohu ('fish'), or from Ambika/Amba.

b_ujhani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; a medieval/modern town in Budaun district, Uttar Pradesh.
b_ujhani.etymology_analysis: Local Hindi toponym in Budaun district without pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation.

b_bachhraon.first_mention_attestation: Earliest dated monument is a mosque built in 1288 CE during the reign of Delhi Sultan Mu'izz ud-Din Kaiqubad; later recorded in the Ain-i-Akbari.
b_bachhraon.etymology_analysis: Medieval Hindi toponym in Amroha district, attested from the late 13th century CE.

b_vodamayutja.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Vodamayuta in a 12th-century CE Rashtrakuta stone inscription from Budaun (listing twelve kings; tradition places its founding around 905 CE).
b_vodamayutja.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vodamayuta (also Vedamooth in an 11th-century CE inscription), the medieval predecessor name of Budaun.

b_ahichatra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ahichchhatra on Panchala coinage (c. 2nd–1st century BCE), in the Mahabharata, and visited by Xuanzang in the 7th century CE.
b_ahichatra.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Ahichchhatra ('Serpent Canopy'), ancient capital of North Panchala.

b_tilokpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; a village in Tilhar, Uttar Pradesh (distinct from Trilokpur in Himachal Pradesh).
b_tilokpur.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Trilokapura ('Town of the Three Worlds'), vernacularized to Tilokpur.

b_bareily.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1537 CE by Bansdeo and Bareldeo (or Jagat Singh Katehriya) in the Katehar region.
b_bareily.eponym_details: Named after Bareldeo, one of the two Katehriya Rajput brothers (Bansdeo and Bareldeo) credited with founding the city in 1537 CE.
b_bareily.etymology_analysis: Named after Bareldeo (or Bans-Bareli), founded in 1537 CE in Bareilly district.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Panchala coinage (c. 2nd century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ahichchhatra (in modern Bareilly district) was the ancient capital of North Panchala prior to the medieval foundation of Bareilly.

b_dhamalpur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1539 CE regional chronicles as Dhamalpur (modern Dhrol in Gujarat), the seat of Dhamal Chavda prior to its conquest and renaming by Jam Hardholji.
b_dhamalpur.eponym_details: Named after Dhamal Chavda, the local Chavda Rajput chieftain who ruled Dhamalpur before his defeat by Jam Hardholji in 1539 CE.
b_dhamalpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of the chieftain's personal name Dhamal and the settlement suffix -pur ('town'), denoting the Chavda stronghold later renamed Dhrol in 1539 CE.

b_morvi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; attested as a medieval/princely state capital (Morvi/Morbi) in Kathiawar.
b_morvi.etymology_analysis: Gujarati toponym Morvi/Morbi, traditionally linked to mor ('peacock') or Mayurapuri.

b_lakhota.first_mention_attestation: Lakhota Lake and Palace in Jamnagar were constructed after the founding of Jamnagar (Nawanagar) by Jam Rawalji Jadeja in 1540 CE.
b_lakhota.etymology_analysis: Toponym of Lakhota Lake and fort in Jamnagar, dating to the Nawanagar period (post-1540 CE).

b_halvad.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the capital of Jhalavad (Dhrangadhra State) by Rajodharji Jhala around 1488 CE.
b_halvad.etymology_analysis: Gujarati toponym Halvad, traditionally said to be shaped like a plow (hal) or derived from a banyan grove.

b_dvaraka.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dvaraka / Dvaravati in the Mahabharata and early Buddhist/Jain texts (c. 4th–2nd century BCE).
b_dvaraka.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Dvaraka ('City of Gates', from dvara 'gate'), the sacred coastal city of Krishna in Saurashtra.

b_lalpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; a modern/late-medieval town in Jamnagar district, Gujarat.
b_lalpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Lal (red or a personal name) and pur ('town').

b_bhanvad.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1313 CE by Jethwa ruler Rana Bhanji Jethwa of Ghumli after the sack of Ghumli.
b_bhanvad.eponym_details: Named after Rana Bhanji Jethwa, who founded the fortified town in 1313 CE.
b_bhanvad.etymology_analysis: Named after Rana Bhanji Jethwa (Bhan + vad, 'settlement/banyan of Bhanji') in 1313 CE.

b_kanthakota.first_mention_attestation: Historically attested as the hilltop fortress of Kanthadurg / Kanthakota (Kanthkot in Kutch, Gujarat), where Chaulukya king Mularaja took refuge c. 950 CE and Bhima I sheltered from Mahmud of Ghazni in 1024 CE (later Kutch tradition attributes initial fort walls to Samvat 900 / 843 CE, without contemporary pre-867 epigraphy).
b_kanthakota.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Kanthakota (Gujarati Kanthkot, also Kanthadurg), traditionally named after the ascetic Kanthadnath combined with kota ('fort'), referring to the ancient hilltop stronghold in Bhachau, Kutch.

b_bhuj.first_mention_attestation: Established by Rao Hamir in 1510 CE and made the capital of Kutch by Rao Khengarji I in 1549 CE.
b_bhuj.etymology_analysis: Named after Bhujia Hill (from Sanskrit Bhujanga, 'serpent', associated with serpent worship at Bhujang Dev).

b_anjar_kutch.first_mention_attestation: Early surviving inscriptions at Anjar date from the 16th century CE onward; local folklore attributing its founding to 650 CE (Samvat 707) by Ajepal ('brother of the king of Ajmer') is anachronistic, as Ajmer was founded in the early 12th century CE (c. 1113 CE).
b_anjar_kutch.etymology_analysis: Traditionally linked to Ajepal (Ajayapala), who is credited in local Kutch chronicles with settling Anjar in 650 CE.

b_khetaka.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Khetaka in Katyayana's Varttika (c. 2nd century BCE) and in Maitraka copper-plate grants (5th–8th century CE) as a major regional center.
b_khetaka.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Khetaka ('fortified village/town'), modern Kheda in Gujarat.

b_khambhat.first_mention_attestation: First contemporarily attested by Arab geographer Al-Mas'udi in 915–916 CE as Kambaya (later Sanskritized as Stambhatirtha in medieval Chaulukya-era texts).
b_khambhat.etymology_analysis: Derived from Prakrit khambha (Sanskrit stambha, 'pillar'), corresponding to the medieval Sanskrit name Stambhatirtha.

b_dholka.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the early 13th century CE as Dhavalgadh / Dhavalakka, the seat of Vaghela founder Vir Dhaval.
b_dholka.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Sanskrit Dhavalakka/Dhavalgadh ('White Fort' or fort of Dhavala) into Gujarati Dholka.

b_ashaval.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological and historical evidence attests Ashaval (Ashapalli) from the 11th century CE, when Chaulukya king Karna I defeated the Bhil chieftain of Ashaval and founded Karnavati nearby.
b_ashaval.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Ashapalli ('settlement of Asha'), evolving into Ashaval, the medieval predecessor of Ahmedabad.

b_mohadavasaka.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mohadavasaka in the 949 CE Harsola copper plates of Paramara king Siyaka II (and later in inscriptions of Bhoja).
b_mohadavasaka.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Mohadavasaka ('dwelling/district of Mohada'), modern Modasa in Aravalli district, Gujarat.

b_jhalod.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; a medieval/modern town in Dahod district, Gujarat.
b_jhalod.etymology_analysis: Gujarati toponym in Dahod district without pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation.

b_idar.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally referred to as Ilva Durga (Idar Fort) in the Mahabharata and Puranic traditions (c. 300 BCE traditional epic horizon), though recovered stone inscriptions at Idar begin in the 12th century CE.
b_idar.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Ilvadurga ('Fort of Ilvala'), contracted in Prakrit and Gujarati to Idar.

b_anahilapataka.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 746 CE by Vanaraja Chavda as the capital of the Chavda dynasty of Gujarat (recorded in medieval Gujarati prabandha chronicles such as Merutunga's Prabandhachintamani and later Chaulukya inscriptions as Anahilapataka / Anahilavada, modern Patan).

morphemes.translation: personal name of the 8th-century shepherd Anahila

b_anahilapataka.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Anahilapataka ('Town of Anahila', also Anahilavada / Anhilwara, modern Patan), traditionally named by Vanaraja Chavda in 746 CE after his shepherd guide Anahila.

b_vadnagar.first_mention_attestation: The medieval name Vadnagar ('Great Town') replaced the pre-867 CE names Anartapura and Anandapura (attested in 505–648 CE Maitraka grants and Xuanzang 640 CE).
b_vadnagar.etymology_analysis: Gujarati Vadnagar (from Vriddhanagara, 'Old/Great City'), the later medieval name of ancient Anandapura.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Maitraka copper-plate grants of Valabhi (505–648 CE) and Xuanzang (640 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Vadnagar is firmly identified with ancient Anandapura / Anartapura, visited by Xuanzang in 640 CE and named in Maitraka land grants.

b_siddhapura.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Siddhapura after Chaulukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja (r. 1092–1142 CE), who completed the Rudra Mahalaya temple there (begun earlier at Śrīsthala by Mularaja in 943 CE).
b_siddhapura.eponym_details: Named Siddhapura after Chaulukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja (r. 1092–1142 CE), who completed the Rudra Mahalaya temple there.
b_siddhapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Siddhapura ('City of Siddha / Siddharaja'), replacing the earlier name Sristhala.

b_modhera.first_mention_attestation: First firmly dated by the Chaulukya-era Sun Temple built in 1026–1027 CE (Vikram Samvat 1083) during the reign of Bhima I.
b_modhera.etymology_analysis: Associated with the Modha Brahmins/Banias and Goddess Modheshwari (Sanskrit Dharmaranya in Puranic tradition).

b_kamboika.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kamboika in 10th-century CE records (Bühler, Indian Antiquary VI, 1877); modern Kamboi in Patan district, Gujarat.
b_kamboika.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Kambojika ('pertaining to the Kambojas'), evolving into Kamboika and modern Kamboi.

b_daman.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Damana in the Nashik Cave inscription of Western Kshatrapa ruler Nahapana (c. 120 CE).
b_daman.etymology_analysis: From ancient Damana (attested in the 2nd-century CE Nashik inscription), giving its name to the coastal territory of Daman.

b_sanjan.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as the port of Sindān (identified with Sanjan) in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan during the reign of Caliph al-Ma'mun (809–813 / c. 813 CE, captured by al-Fadl ibn Mahan), prior to Amoghavarsha I's 871 CE Sanjan copper-plate grant.

morphemes.translation: Sanjan (port town, possibly linked to Khorasan Sanjan)

b_sanjan.etymology_analysis: Early medieval port in southern Gujarat attested in Rashtrakuta copper plates (871 CE), traditionally associated with Zoroastrian refugees in the Qissa-i Sanjan.

b_akruresvara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Akrureshvara-vishaya (an administrative district) in the copper-plate land grants of Gurjara ruler Dadda II (629–643 CE), and subsequently in 8th–9th century CE Rashtrakuta copper-plate charters.

morphemes.translation: gentle, not cruel (or legendary sage/shrine name)

b_akruresvara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Akrureshvara ('Lord Akrura', modern Ankleshwar in Bharuch district, Gujarat), attested as an administrative center (vishaya) in 7th–9th century CE Gurjara and Rashtrakuta charters.

b_navasarika.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Navasarika in the 738–739 CE Navsari copper-plate inscription of Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin of the Gujarat Chalukyas (and earlier Chalukya charters from the region beginning in 671 CE).
b_navasarika.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Navasarika (modern Navsari in southern Gujarat), capital of the 7th–8th century CE Early Chalukyas of Navasarika in Lata.

b_bharuch.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Barygaza in the 1st-century CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (and Bargosa in Strabo's Geography), corresponding to Sanskrit Bhrigukachchha / Pali Bharukachchha.
b_bharuch.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Bhrigukachchha (or Prakrit/Pali Bharukachchha), meaning 'shore/marsh of the sage Bhrigu', rendered in Greco-Roman sources as Barygaza and Bargosa, and later contracted to Bharuch.

b_tadkeshwar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; local tradition records the settlement as Bhim-Nagar under Chaulukya king Bhima I (11th century CE) prior to its later name Tadkeshwar.
b_tadkeshwar.etymology_analysis: Also spelled Tarkeshwar, traditionally linked to Tadkeshwar Mahadev ('Lord Shiva of the sun/open sky'). No contemporary attestation of the name exists prior to 867 CE.

b_rajpipla.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 1340 CE with the establishment of the Gohil Rajput Kingdom of Rajpipla.
b_rajpipla.etymology_analysis: Compound of Sanskrit/Gujarati raja ('royal, king') and pipla ('pipal tree'), referring to a royal settlement marked by pipal trees.

b_nandurbar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Nandurbar appears in late medieval Khandesh/Farooqui Sultanate records (14th–15th century CE), while earlier local tradition links it to Nandanagri.
b_nandurbar.etymology_analysis: Locally derived either from a traditional ruler Nandaraja (Nandanagri) or from nandar ('agricultural marketplace'). A 3rd-century CE Kanheri inscription mentions Nandigriha, but its identification with Nandurbar is conjectural.

b_vadodara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Vadapadraka in the 812 CE Rashtrakuta copper-plate grant of Karka II (Suvarnavarsha) of Lata.
b_vadodara.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Vatapadraka / Vadapadraka ('village of banyan trees'), which evolved into Gujarati Vadodara.

b_kayavarohan.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 2nd century CE as Kayavarohana (modern Karvan), the birthplace of the Pashupata Shaiva teacher Lakulisha, corroborated by 2nd-century CE excavated sculptures and relics.
b_kayavarohan.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Kayavarohana ('descent of the body'), referring to the Shaiva tradition that Shiva descended into a human body (Lakulisha) at this site.

b_darbhavati.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Darbhavati in the 6th-century CE astronomical treatise Romaka Siddhanta.
b_darbhavati.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Darbhavati ('abounding in darbha/kusha grass'), which later evolved into the Gujarati tadbhava form Dabhoi.

b_vamanasthali.first_mention_attestation: Earliest surviving local epigraphic record is the Vanthali stone inscription of VS 1346 (1289–1290 CE), while Hemachandra's 12th-century Dvyashraya Kavya and bardic chronicles record Vamanasthali as the capital of 10th-century Abhira ruler Graharipu and the Chudasama dynasty (traditionally founded c. 875 CE).
b_vamanasthali.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vamanasthali ('Abode/Place of Vamana', contracted to modern Vanthali in Junagadh district, Gujarat), medieval capital of the Chudasama dynasty in Saurashtra.

b_bhumilka.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bhutambilika / Bhumilika in Saindhava dynasty copper-plate grants (c. 735–920 CE) as their capital in western Saurashtra, Gujarat.

morphemes.translation: ancient toponym contracted to Bhumilika / Ghumli

b_bhumilka.etymology_analysis: Contracted form of Sanskrit Bhutambilika / Bhumilika (later Bhumli and modern Ghumli in Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat), attested from c. 735 CE as the Saindhava capital.

b_shrinagar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the capital of the Jethwa dynasty from 1218–1220 CE before Rana Shiyaji moved the capital to Ghumli in 1220 CE.
b_shrinagar.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Shrinagara ('auspicious city' or 'city of Shri/Lakshmi'). Although 6th-century Sun temple ruins exist nearby, the place name Shrinagar is not attested in contemporary pre-867 CE records.

b_mangrol.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mangalapura in the 1145 CE Mangrol stone inscription of the Guhila feudatory Muluka under Chaulukya king Kumarapala.
b_mangrol.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Mangalapura ('auspicious city'), which contracted in Gujarati to Mangrol.

b_uperkot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by this name <= 867 CE; the fort on the Junagadh plateau was abandoned in the 6th century CE and rebuilt by Chudasama ruler Graharipu in the 10th century CE, with Uparkot appearing as a medieval Gujarati name.
b_uperkot.etymology_analysis: From Gujarati upar ('upper') + kot ('fort'), meaning 'upper fort', referring to the citadel of ancient Girinagara (modern Junagadh).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts at Girnar (c. 250 BCE) and Rudradaman I's Junagadh rock inscription (150 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Girinagara (Junagadh/Girnar) is attested from the Mauryan era before the medieval name Uparkot.

b_somnath.first_mention_attestation: The temple/toponym Somanatha (Somnath) is explicitly attested in 11th-century CE accounts (Mahmud of Ghazni's 1024–1026 CE raid) and later prabandha tradition (13th-century Prabhavakacharita); Nagabhata II's 815 CE Buchkala inscription is in Jodhpur rather than Somnath, while the ancient site itself was known as Prabhāsa.
b_somnath.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Somanatha ('Lord of the Moon'), an epithet of Shiva worshipped at the coastal shrine of Prabhasa Patan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Nasik cave inscription of Ushavadata (c. 120 CE) and Mahabharata
older_name_by_867.notes: The sacred coastal site at Somnath is attested as Prabhāsa (Prabhasa-tirtha) in the Mahabharata and Ushavadata's 2nd-century CE Nasik inscription prior to the medieval name Somanatha / Somnath.

b_delvada.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_delvada.etymology_analysis: Derived from Gujarati deval ('temple') + vada ('settlement/enclosure'), meaning 'temple settlement'.

b_saymur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Saimur / Saymur in the 10th-century CE accounts of Arab geographers, beginning with al-Mas'udi (c. 915 CE), referring to the port of Chaul.
b_saymur.etymology_analysis: Saymur (or Saimur) is the medieval Arabic adaptation of the Konkan port name Chemula / Simylla (modern Chaul).

b_moherak.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1026–1027 CE in the Sun Temple inscription of Chaulukya king Bhima I at Modhera (historically Moheraka / Modheraka).
b_moherak.etymology_analysis: Moherak reflects the Sanskritized form Moheraka / Modheraka, the historical name of Modhera in northern Gujarat.

b_valabhi.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 475 CE as Valabhi / Vallabhi, the capital of the Maitraka dynasty, in Maitraka copper-plate grants and 7th-century CE Chinese pilgrims' accounts.
b_valabhi.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit valabhi ('pavilion, pinnacle, vaulted roof'), the name of the major Maitraka capital and Buddhist university center in Saurashtra.

b_shatrunjaya.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Jain texts from the 5th century CE onwards as Shatrunjaya, the sacred hill near Palitana.
b_shatrunjaya.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Shatrunjaya ('conqueror of enemies'), referring to the sacred Jain hill near Palitana where inner spiritual enemies are overcome.

b_dhandhuka.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1088 CE as the birthplace of the Jain scholar and polymath Acharya Hemachandra.
b_dhandhuka.etymology_analysis: Toponym in the Bhal region of Gujarat, attested from the late 11th century CE as the birthplace of Acharya Hemachandra.

b_sihor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by the name Sihor <= 867 CE; some historians identify it with Sinhapura of ancient Pali chronicles, though that identification remains debated.
b_sihor.etymology_analysis: Sihor is derived from Sanskrit Simhapura ('lion city') via Prakrit Sihapura, though its identification with the Sinhapura of the Pali chronicles is disputed.

b_vardhamana.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Vardhamana (modern Wadhwan) in Jinasena's Harivamsha Purana (783 CE) and in Dharanivaraha's Haddala copper-plate grant (914 CE).
b_vardhamana.etymology_analysis: Named Vardhamana (or Vardhamanapura) after Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th Jain Tirthankara, later evolving into Gujarati Wadhwan.

b_ranpur.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the early 14th century CE (c. 1313 CE), when it was founded by Gohil Rajput chieftain Ranaji Gohil.
b_ranpur.eponym_details: Named after Ranaji Gohil (early 14th century CE), a Gohil Rajput chieftain who founded the town around 1313 CE.
b_ranpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of the founder's name Ranaji Gohil and Sanskrit-derived -pur ('town, city'), founded in the early 14th century CE.

b_amarvalli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary dated pre-867 CE inscriptions; Amarvalli is cited in later tradition as an ancient Sanskrit name of Amreli.
b_amarvalli.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit amara ('immortal') + valli ('creeper'), cited as the classical Sanskritized form of Amreli, though lacking contemporary pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation.

b_bajura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Bajura appears later as one of the medieval Baise Rajya principalities of western Nepal.
b_bajura.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the medieval Baise Rajya principality in far-western Nepal; 'Badschûre' in the repository is a Germanized transcription.

b_simikot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_simikot.etymology_analysis: Himalayan settlement name in Humla District ending in Nepali kot ('fort, stronghold'); unattested before 867 CE.

b_dang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE written sources; Dang later appears as a medieval Baise Rajya principality in the Inner Terai.
b_dang.etymology_analysis: Name of the large Inner Terai valley (Dang Valley) and medieval Baise Rajya principality in mid-western Nepal.

b_gulariya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_gulariya.etymology_analysis: Terai toponym in Bardiya District derived from gular ('cluster fig tree') with the locative suffix -iya; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_jagatipur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Jagatipur served as the early seat of the medieval Jajarkot kingdom in the Baise Rajya confederation.

morphemes.translation: world, earth, or personal name Jagat

b_jagatipur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Jagati and -pur ('town, city'); 'Dschagatipur' in the repository is a Germanized transliteration.

b_rukum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Rukum appears later as a medieval Baise Rajya principality.
b_rukum.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the medieval Baise Rajya principality of Rukum (centered on Rukumkot) in western Nepal.

b_gautamkot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; associated with the medieval Baise Rajya principality of Atbis Gotam (Gutam).
b_gautamkot.etymology_analysis: Compound of Gautam (Gotam) and Nepali kot ('fort, stronghold'), referring to the medieval hill fort in West Rukum.

b_sinja.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 12th–14th centuries CE in Khasa Malla royal records and Karnali cliff/pillar inscriptions as the capital valley (Sinja / Simja) of the medieval Khasa Malla kingdom in western Nepal.

morphemes.translation: historic valley and capital name (Sinja / Simja)

b_sinja.etymology_analysis: Sinja (also Simja), the historic Karnali valley in Jumla district, western Nepal, which served as the imperial capital of the Khasa Malla kingdom from the 12th to 14th centuries CE.

b_jumla.first_mention_attestation: Attested historically as the center of the Kallala Kingdom of Jumla founded c. 1404 CE by Baliraja following the breakup of the Khasa Malla empire; unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources.

morphemes.translation: historic mountain valley and town name in Karnali

b_jumla.etymology_analysis: Jumla is the historic high-altitude town and kingdom in the Karnali basin of western Nepal, prominent from the late Khasa Malla and Kallala eras onward.

b_dullu.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1354–1357 CE in Devanagari stone inscriptions and Prithvi Malla's pillar inscription at Dullu, winter capital of the Khasa Malla kingdom.
b_dullu.etymology_analysis: Dullu was the winter capital of the Khasa Malla kingdom in Dailekh District, attested in 14th-century CE royal inscriptions.

b_kaski.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Kaski appears as a medieval Chaubisi Rajya principality in central Nepal.

morphemes.translation: principality name Kaski, traditionally linked to Khas

b_kaski.etymology_analysis: Hypothesized to derive from the ethnonym Khas / Cas ('referring to Khas rulers'), naming the medieval Chaubisi Rajya principality in the Pokhara valley.

b_tanahun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Tanahun appears later as a medieval Chaubisi Rajya principality.
b_tanahun.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the medieval Chaubisi Rajya principality of Tanahun in central Nepal; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_gorkha.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1559 CE, when Dravya Shah conquered Liglig and renamed the kingdom Gorkha after the Nath yogi Gorakhnath.
b_gorkha.eponym_details: Named after the Nath yogi saint Gorakhnath (c. 11th–12th century CE), who is venerated at a cave in Gorkha.
b_gorkha.etymology_analysis: Derived from the name of the medieval Nath yogi saint Gorakhnath (Gorakshanatha), adopted when Dravya Shah established the Gorkha Kingdom in 1559 CE.

b_lumbini.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Mauryan Emperor Ashoka's Rummindei Brahmi pillar inscription at Lumbini, dated c. 249 BCE.

morphemes.translation: sacred grove and birthplace of Gautama Buddha

b_lumbini.etymology_analysis: Ancient Prakrit/Sanskrit toponym attested on Ashoka's c. 249 BCE pillar inscription (Lummini-game) marking the birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama.

b_gulmi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Gulmi appears later as a medieval Chaubisi Rajya principality.

morphemes.translation: principality name Gulmi (cf. Sanskrit gulma, military outpost/thicket)

b_gulmi.etymology_analysis: Name of the medieval Chaubisi Rajya principality of Gulmi in western-central Nepal; unattested before 867 CE.

b_doti.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 13th century CE as one of the eight successor principalities formed after the disintegration of the Katyuri Kingdom.

morphemes.translation: regional name, traditionally from Dovati ('between two rivers')

b_doti.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Dovati ('land between two rivers') or Dev-atavi; attested as an independent kingdom in far-western Nepal from the 13th century CE.

b_godawari.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_godawari.etymology_analysis: Named after the local Godavari River in Kailali District, itself named from Sanskrit Godavari ('giver of water/cattle').

b_baitadi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_baitadi.etymology_analysis: Toponym of Baitadi District in far-western Nepal; unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources.

b_devalgarh.first_mention_attestation: Historically documented in 1512 CE when Panwar king Ajay Pal transferred the capital of the unified Garhwal Kingdom to Devalgarh, a fortified seat traditionally founded by King Deval of Kangra.
b_devalgarh.eponym_details: Named after King Deval (traditionally a prince/ruler from Kangra) who founded the fortified seat in Pauri Garhwal prior to its adoption as capital by Garhwal king Ajay Pal in 1512 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name King Deval (or temple, devala)

b_devalgarh.etymology_analysis: Compound of the personal name Deval and Garhwali/Hindi garh ('fort'), referring to the historic Panwar Garhwal seat in Pauri Garhwal, Uttarakhand.

b_srinagar.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 1517 CE, when Raja Ajay Pal transferred the capital of the Garhwal Kingdom from Devalgarh to Srinagar.
b_srinagar.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Shrinagara ('auspicious city'), established as the Garhwal capital in the early 16th century CE.

b_dehradun.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 17th century CE, following Baba Ram Rai's establishment of his dera (camp/shrine) in the Doon Valley.
b_dehradun.etymology_analysis: Compound of Hindi dehra ('shrine, camp') and dun ('valley'), referring to the camp/shrine of Guru Ram Rai in the Doon Valley.

b_uttarkashi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by the name Uttarkashi <= 867 CE; the town was historically known as Barahat prior to the modern/Sanskritic designation Uttarkashi.
b_uttarkashi.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Uttarakashi ('Northern Kashi'), a directional/analogical compound comparing the Bhagirathi pilgrimage town to Varanasi ('Uttarkaschi' in the repository is a Germanized spelling).

b_champawat.first_mention_attestation: Earliest dated epigraphic record at Champawat is the 1223 CE Baleshwar Temple inscription of Krachalla Deva (while later Kumaoni vamshavali tradition attributes the founding of the Chand capital there to Som Chand in the 10th–11th century CE).
b_champawat.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Champavati ('Place of Champa'), the first capital of the medieval Chand dynasty in Kumaon, Uttarakhand.

b_bhimtal.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 13th century CE, when Chand ruler Trilok Chand built a fort at Bhimtal.
b_bhimtal.etymology_analysis: Named after Bhimtal Lake, a compound of Bhima (the Mahabharata hero) and Hindi tal ('lake').

b_kartikeyapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Karttikeyapura in the Pandukeshwar copper-plate inscriptions of Katyuri ruler Lalitasuradeva (dated December 853 / September 854 CE) and other 8th–10th century CE Katyuri copper-plate charters.

morphemes.translation: Karttikeya (Hindu war deity, son of Shiva)

b_kartikeyapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Karttikeyapura ('City of Karttikeya'), the early medieval capital of the Katyuri dynasty in Uttarakhand (associated with Joshimath and Baijnath), attested in 9th-century copper plates.

b_almora.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1568 CE (or 1563 CE), when Chand king Kalyan Chand founded the town as the new capital of Kumaon.
b_almora.etymology_analysis: Derived from Kumaoni bhilmora / kilmora (a sorrel plant gathered by local Tewaris for the Katarmal Sun Temple, giving the name Almori/Almora); earlier called Rajapur and Alamnagar.

b_askot.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1279 CE, when Abhay Pal Deo of a Katyuri branch established the Rajwar principality at Askot.
b_askot.etymology_analysis: From Assi Kot ('eighty forts'), referring to the eighty hill forts traditionally held by the Askot rulers.

b_ilam.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 18th century CE (independent Limbu kingdom until 1714 CE; Gorkha-Limbuwan treaty of 1774 CE; Ilam Bazar established in 1818 CE).
b_ilam.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Limbu language il ('twisted') + lam ('road'), meaning 'winding road'.

b_panchthar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE written sources; Panchthar (Panthar) is one of the historical territories of Limbuwan.
b_panchthar.etymology_analysis: From Nepali panch ('five') + thar ('clan'), referring to the five Limbu clans of the Panthar territory in Limbuwan.

b_gograha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Gograha Bazaar was the earlier name of Biratnagar prior to its 20th-century renaming.
b_gograha.etymology_analysis: Earlier local name (Gograha Bazaar) of modern Biratnagar in eastern Nepal; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_khotang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_khotang.etymology_analysis: Toponym of Khotang District in eastern Nepal ('Chotang' in the repository is a Germanized spelling); unattested before 867 CE.

b_okhaldhunga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_okhaldhunga.etymology_analysis: From Nepali okhal ('mortar') + dhunga ('stone'), meaning 'mortar stone'; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_dolakha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Dolakha appears in medieval Malla-period records of Nepal Mandala.
b_dolakha.etymology_analysis: Historic Newar settlement (Dwalkha) on the eastern trade route to Tibet, prominent during the medieval Malla period; unattested in dated pre-867 CE sources.

b_yangwarok.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE written sources; Yangwarok (Yangrok) was one of the ten traditional Limbuwan kingdoms.
b_yangwarok.etymology_analysis: Traditional Limbuwan principality name ('Jangwaroch' in the repository is a Germanized transcription); unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE written records.

b_dhankuta.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_dhankuta.etymology_analysis: Nepali compound from dhan ('paddy/rice') + kuta ('pounding/granary'); unattested before 867 CE.

b_bhojpur_tibet.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_bhojpur_tibet.etymology_analysis: According to the District Coordination Committee Bhojpur, named for the Himalayan birch (bhojpatra, Betula utilis) found abundantly in the area + -pur ('town, city').

b_bhaktapur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bhaktapur in an inscription dated 928 CE (and Khwopa in a 1004 CE manuscript), while the site's earlier non-Sanskrit name Khopring appears in a Licchavi Sanskrit stone inscription of 594 CE.
b_bhaktapur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Bhaktapura ('city of devotees'), also called Bhaktagrama (Hindi/Nepali Bhatgaon); its Licchavi-era name Khopring (modern Newar Khwopa) is attested in 594 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Licchavi dynasty Sanskrit stone inscription at Gomarhi, Bhaktapur (594 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Khopring (ancestor of Newar Khwopa) is attested in a 594 CE Licchavi inscription prior to the 928 CE attestation of Bhaktapur.

b_lalitpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by the Sanskrit name Lalitpur in contemporary pre-867 CE inscriptions; historically known as Yala in Newar and Patan in Sanskrit.
b_lalitpur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Lalitapura / Lalitapattana ('city of beauty/grace'), alongside the indigenous Newar name Yala and Sanskrit Patan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Licchavi-period inscriptions at Patan (6th–7th centuries CE, e.g., 613 CE / Yūpagrāma)
older_name_by_867.notes: Historically known in Newar as Yala (from Licchavi Yūpagrāma) and in Sanskrit/Nepali as Patan in Licchavi inscriptions (6th–7th centuries CE) prior to the later Sanskrit name Lalitpur.

b_dhulikhel.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_dhulikhel.etymology_analysis: Derived from Newar dhalikhela ('yogurt field', modern Newar dhaukhyo), also traditionally linked to Sanskrit Dhawalasrotapura.

b_janakpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the early 18th century CE (earliest written description as a pilgrimage site dates to 1805 CE), retrospectively identified with the ancient Videha capital.
b_janakpur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Janakapura ('city of King Janaka'), named after the legendary Videha ruler Janaka ('Dschanakpur' in the repository is a Germanized spelling).

b_rajbiraj.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1944 CE, when the district headquarters of Saptari was transferred from Hanumannagar to Rajbiraj (named after the 14th-century CE Rajdevi temple).
b_rajbiraj.etymology_analysis: Named after the Rajdevi temple rebuilt by the Sena kings in the early 14th century CE, and planned as a modern town in 1944 CE.

b_kathmandu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kasthamandapa in a manuscript colophon dated 1143 CE (during the reign of Narendradeva), while Gunakama Deva founded Kantipur in the late 10th century CE.
b_kathmandu.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Kasthamandapa ('wooden pavilion'), the historic public rest-house (sattal) at Maru Tole whose name expanded to the unified city.

b_kirtipur.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 1099 CE, when Thakuri king Shivadeva III (r. 1099–1126 CE) founded Kirtipur.
b_kirtipur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Kirtipura ('glorious city'), founded by Shivadeva III in 1099 CE (colloquially Kipoo in Newar).

b_hetauda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; attested in modern Nepalese administrative records (20th century CE).
b_hetauda.etymology_analysis: Nepali Heṭaũḍā; local tradition associates the name with Hiḍimbā from the Mahābhārata, though no pre-modern historical attestation confirms this.

b_bharatpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; developed during 20th-century Chitwan resettlement and incorporated as a municipality in 1979 CE.
b_bharatpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Bharata and Sanskrit-derived -pur ('town, city'); modern Chitwan settlement.

b_allai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in modern Pakistani administrative records (20th–21st century CE).
b_allai.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the Allai Valley in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, of local Dardic/Pashto origin.

b_waihind.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Waihind/Vayhand in 10th–11th century CE Islamic geographical works (Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam, 982 CE; al-Bīrūnī, 1030 CE).
b_waihind.etymology_analysis: Medieval Perso-Arabic form of Sanskrit Udabhāṇḍapura (also Uḍakhāṇḍa), the Hindu Shahi capital on the Indus (modern Hund).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (645 CE, as Wu-to-chia-han-cha / Udakhanda)
older_name_by_867.notes: Xuanzang visited the site in 645 CE under the name Udakhanda (Udabhāṇḍapura), before the Perso-Arabic form Waihind appeared in the 10th–11th centuries CE.

b_kaghan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern British colonial and Pakistani gazetteers (19th–20th century CE).
b_kaghan.etymology_analysis: Alpine valley name in Mansehra District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_chilas.first_mention_attestation: Although Buddhist and Kharoshthi/Brahmi rock carvings at the site date to the 1st–7th centuries CE, the toponym Chilas itself is unattested in pre-867 CE texts.

morphemes.translation: Chilas (local settlement name, possibly linked to chilíi juniper)

b_chilas.etymology_analysis: Dardic/Shina toponym in Gilgit-Baltistan; local tradition links the Chilíis/Chilas name to a species of juniper (chilíi).

b_astore.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in later Kashmiri/colonial historical accounts (19th century CE).
b_astore.etymology_analysis: Dardic valley toponym in Gilgit-Baltistan; no pre-867 CE textual attestation.

b_minimarg.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in modern Kashmiri and Pakistani records (20th century CE).
b_minimarg.etymology_analysis: From Kashmiri menee ('frog') + marg ('meadow', cf. Sanskrit maṭha/mārga), meaning 'Meadow of Frogs'.

b_srinagara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the capital of Kashmir in Xuanzang's 631 CE travel account (Si-Yu-Ki) and detailed in Kalhana's Rajatarangini, which records both Ashoka's older capital Srinagari (Pandrethan) and Pravarasena II's 6th-century CE new capital Pravarapura that assumed the name Srinagara.
b_srinagara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Srinagara ('City of Prosperity / Sri', modern Srinagar), the ancient capital of Kashmir on the Jhelum River, attested by Xuanzang in 631 CE and in Kalhana's Rajatarangini.

b_parihasapura.first_mention_attestation: First attested by name in Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī (1148 CE), which attributes its founding to Karkota king Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa (r. c. 724–760 CE); no contemporary pre-867 CE inscription naming Parihāsapura survives.
b_parihasapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Parihāsapura, 'City of Laughter/Mirth', founded by Karkota ruler Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa in the 8th century CE.

b_amaresvara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Amareśvara in the Sanskrit Nīlamata Purāṇa (c. 6th–7th century CE) and later in Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī (1148 CE).
b_amaresvara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Amareśvara ('Immortal Lord', i.e., Shiva), referring to the sacred cave shrine of Amarnath in Kashmir.

b_gilgit.first_mention_attestation: The modern form Gilgit (from local Gilit) is unattested in pre-867 CE sources; Chinese Tang records (c. 645–722 CE) refer to the polity as Little Bolü (Bolor).

morphemes.translation: Gilgit (local name, possibly from Sanskrit giri 'mountain')

b_gilgit.etymology_analysis: Local Shina name Gilit (earlier Sargīn), later standardized as Gilgit; the valley was a Buddhist center under the Patola Shahis (5th–8th century CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xuanzang (627–645 CE) and Tang dynasty chronicles as Little Bolü (Bolor)
older_name_by_867.notes: Pre-867 CE Chinese and Islamic sources refer to the Gilgit Valley as Little Bolor (Xiao Bolü) or Burushal.

b_baltit.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; Baltit Fort and town are documented from the 17th century CE (rebuilt in Balti style under Mir Ayesho II).
b_baltit.etymology_analysis: Historic capital of the Hunza Valley (renamed Karimabad in the 20th century), associated with Balti architectural influence.

b_tashkurgan.first_mention_attestation: The Turkic name Tashkurgan ('Stone Fort') is post-867 CE; in pre-867 CE sources the oasis was known as Puli (Hanshu, 1st–2nd century CE) and Jiepantuo/Khavandha (Song Yun 500 CE; Xuanzang 649 CE).
b_tashkurgan.etymology_analysis: From Turkic tash ('stone') + kurgan ('fortress, mound'), meaning 'Stone Fortress' (Chinese Shitoucheng).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 111 CE) as Kingdom of Puli, and Xuanzang (649 CE) as Jiepantuo
older_name_by_867.notes: Also identified by some scholars with Ptolemy's Lithinos Pyrgos ('Stone Tower', c. 150 CE).

b_golaghmuli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in modern Gilgit-Baltistan geographical records.
b_golaghmuli.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the Golaghmuli Valley in Ghizer District, Gilgit-Baltistan; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kalam_TARIM.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern Swat Kohistan and Pakistani records.
b_kalam_TARIM.etymology_analysis: Gawri (Kalam Kohistani) toponym in Upper Swat, Pakistan; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_shandur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern colonial and Pakistani records (20th century CE).
b_shandur.etymology_analysis: Name of the high mountain pass (c. 3,720 m) between Chitral and Gilgit-Baltistan; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_yasin.first_mention_attestation: The name Yasin is unattested in pre-867 CE sources; in 721–722 CE Tang Chinese records the valley is attested as Bruzha.
b_yasin.etymology_analysis: High-altitude valley in Gupis-Yasin District, Gilgit-Baltistan; formerly known as Bruzha and Worshigum.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tang dynasty records (721–722 CE) noting Tibetan campaigns against Gilgit and Bruzha
older_name_by_867.notes: Bruzha is attested in 721–722 CE Chinese records for the Yasin Valley.

b_naltar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in modern Gilgit-Baltistan geographical records.
b_naltar.etymology_analysis: Forested valley near Gilgit in Gilgit-Baltistan; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_damoh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a Persian inscription of 1383 CE during Firuz Shah Tughlaq's reign (and a 1480 CE Malwa Sultanate inscription); folk-linked to Rani Damayantī.

morphemes.translation: settlement traditionally named after Rani Damayantī

b_damoh.etymology_analysis: Town in Madhya Pradesh; local tradition derives the name from Rani Damayantī, wife of Raja Nala, though epigraphic attestation begins in 1383 CE.

b_dhamoni.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Mughal-era Āʾīn-i-Akbarī (1590s CE) as a mahal in the sarkar of Raisen, Malwa Subah.
b_dhamoni.etymology_analysis: Fortified settlement in Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, associated with the Garha-Mandla kingdom and Bundela rulers.

b_nohta.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 10th century CE in connection with the Nohleshwar Shiva temple built under Chalukya princess Nohalā Devī, queen of Kalachuri king Yuvarājadeva I.
b_nohta.eponym_details: Named after the 10th-century CE Chalukya princess Nohalā Devī, queen of Kalachuri king Yuvarājadeva I, who patronized the Nohleshwar temple at the site.
b_nohta.etymology_analysis: Derived from the 10th-century Chalukya princess Nohalā Devī, consort of Kalachuri ruler Yuvarājadeva I.

b_kalinjar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kālañjara in the Mahābhārata (c. 4th century BCE–4th century CE) and in early medieval epigraphy including the Nilgund inscription (866 CE).
b_kalinjar.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Kālañjara, a sacred hill fortress in Bundelkhand associated with Shiva as the destroyer of time/decay.

b_khajuraho.first_mention_attestation: First attested by name as Kharjūravāhaka in 10th-century CE Chandela inscriptions (e.g., 954 CE) and as Kajūrāha in al-Bīrūnī (1022 CE); Xuanzang (641 CE) named the region Chi-chi-to (Jejākabhukti) rather than Khajuraho.
b_khajuraho.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Kharjūravāhaka ('date-palm bearer'), referring to the date palms that grew around the Chandela capital.

b_bhatta.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bhatta / Bhatta-Gahora from the 13th century CE with the rise of the Baghel dynasty in Baghelkhand (1234–1236 CE).
b_bhatta.etymology_analysis: Medieval regional and dynastic name (Bhatta-Gahora) for Baghelkhand/Rewa under the Baghel Rajputs from the 13th century CE.

b_umri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in modern central Indian village and district records.
b_umri.etymology_analysis: Hindi/Bundeli settlement name in northern Madhya Pradesh / Bundelkhand, commonly derived from the udumbara (cluster fig) tree.

b_mahoba.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mahotsavanagara in Chandela inscriptions and medieval chronicles from the 10th–12th centuries CE.
b_mahoba.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Sanskrit Mahotsavanagara ('City of the Great Festival/Jubilee'), the medieval capital of the Chandela dynasty.

b_ajaigarh.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Chandela-period inscriptions (11th–13th centuries CE) as Jayapura-Durga, later rendered Ajaigarh.
b_ajaigarh.etymology_analysis: Derived from Chandela Sanskrit Jayapura-Durga ('Fortress of Victory City'), later folk-reinterpreted with gaṛh ('fort') as Ajaigarh.

b_chitrakuta.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Citrakūṭa in Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa (c. 5th–1st century BCE) and depicted in a 3rd-century CE stone panel at Nagarjunakonda.
b_chitrakuta.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Citrakūṭa ('Variegated/Wonderful Peak'), the sacred hill of Rāma's exile on the Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border.

b_rath.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in medieval and modern Uttar Pradesh administrative records.
b_rath.etymology_analysis: Town in Hamirpur district, Uttar Pradesh; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_asni.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Asni pillar inscription of Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Mahīpāladeva dated Samvat 974 (917 CE), and later as a Gahadavala fortress in 1194 CE.

morphemes.translation: Asni (fortified settlement on the Ganges in Fatehpur)

b_asni.etymology_analysis: Historic riverside settlement in Fatehpur district, Uttar Pradesh, attested from the 10th-century Mahīpāladeva inscription.

b_kora.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in late medieval and Mughal-era records (paired with Jahanabad).
b_kora.etymology_analysis: Historic town (Kora Jahanabad) in Fatehpur district, Uttar Pradesh; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_musanagar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by this name in pre-867 CE written sources, though Kushan-era archaeological remains have been excavated nearby.
b_musanagar.etymology_analysis: Compound of Mūsā + Sanskrit-derived nagar ('town'); located on the Yamuna in Kanpur Dehat district.

b_kalpi.first_mention_attestation: First prominently attested in the late 14th century CE as the seat of the Kingdom of Kalpi (c. 1390 CE).
b_kalpi.etymology_analysis: Historic town on the Yamuna in Jalaun district, Uttar Pradesh; seat of a late medieval sultanate from c. 1390 CE.

b_jalaun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in late medieval and Maratha-era records (18th century CE).
b_jalaun.etymology_analysis: Town in Uttar Pradesh that served as the headquarters of the Maratha-era Jalaun State; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_kanyakubja.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kānyakubja in Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya (c. 2nd century BCE) and the Rāmāyaṇa/Mahābhārata, as Kanogiza in Ptolemy (c. 140 CE), and visited by Faxian (5th century CE) and Xuanzang (636 CE).
b_kanyakubja.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Kānyakubja ('[city of] hunchbacked maidens', modern Kannauj), explained in the Rāmāyaṇa by the curse of Vāyu on Kuśanābha's daughters.

b_jajmau.first_mention_attestation: Although the Jajmau mound yielded Painted Grey Ware and a Mauryan-era Brahmi seal (Vasalas), the name Jajmau itself is unattested in pre-867 CE sources.

morphemes.translation: Jajmau (suburb of Kanpur, folk-linked to Yayāti)

b_jajmau.etymology_analysis: Ancient Ganges riverbank site near Kanpur; local tradition links it to King Yayāti, though the name Jajmau is post-867 CE.

b_etawah.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 13th century CE under the Tomaras and Delhi Sultanate; earlier Sanskritized as Iṣṭikāpurī.
b_etawah.etymology_analysis: From Hindi ī̃ṭ ('brick', cf. Sanskrit Iṣṭikāpurī 'brick city'), referring to brick kilns or brick structures along the Yamuna.

b_lakhnau.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lakhanpur / Lakhnau from the 11th century CE; earlier origins are legendary (linked to Lakṣmaṇa of the Rāmāyaṇa).
b_lakhnau.etymology_analysis: Local Awadhi/Hindi Lakhnaū (anglicized Lucknow), traditionally derived from Sanskrit Lakṣmaṇapurī or Lakṣmaṇavatī.

b_jasnaul.first_mention_attestation: According to district tradition, founded before 1000 CE by Raja Jas of the Bhar tribe as Jasnaul (later Barabanki); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_jasnaul.etymology_analysis: Earlier name of Barabanki, traditionally attributed to a Bhar ruler named Raja Jas prior to c. 1000 CE.

b_hardoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in Mughal/colonial-era Awadh records (19th century CE).
b_hardoi.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Sanskrit Haridrohi ('opponent of Hari', linked to Hiranyakaśipu) or Haridvaya ('two incarnations of Hari').

b_manikpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1180 CE by Raja Mānik Chand (Māṇikyacandra), brother of Gahadavala king Jayachandra of Kannauj.
b_manikpur.eponym_details: Named after Raja Manik Chand (Māṇikyacandra, fl. late 12th century CE), brother of Gahadavala ruler Jayachandra of Kannauj.
b_manikpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Raja Mānik Chand + -pur ('town'), founded in the late 12th century CE on the Ganges in Pratapgarh district.

b_lalganj.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; a late medieval/early modern market town (ganj) in Raebareli district.
b_lalganj.etymology_analysis: Compound with Persian-derived -ganj ('market town'), characteristic of late medieval/early modern Awadh toponymy.

b_prayaga.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Prayāga in late Vedic khila hymns, the Mahābhārata (c. 4th century BCE–4th century CE), and the Gupta-era Allahabad Pillar inscription of Samudragupta (c. 350 CE).
b_prayaga.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Prayāga ('place of great sacrifice'), referring to the sacred confluence (Triveṇī Saṅgama) of the Ganga, Yamuna, and mythical Sarasvati.

b_kara.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Kara stone inscription of Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Yaśaḥpāla dated Vikrama Samvat 1093 (1036 CE).
b_kara.etymology_analysis: Medieval town on the Ganges in Kaushambi district, attested from the 1036 CE inscription of Yaśaḥpāla and later the seat of the Delhi Sultanate iqta of Kara-Manikpur.

b_chunar.first_mention_attestation: Earliest recorded history of Chunar Fort as Chunar dates to the 16th century CE (Lodi/Mughal/Sur conflicts); Purāṇic tradition calls the hill Caraṇādri.
b_chunar.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Caraṇādri ('hill of the footprint', associated with Vishnu's Vāmana avatar), shortened in Hindi to Chunār.

b_kantit.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in medieval Gaharwar/zamindari records (16th–18th centuries CE). Identification with Purāṇic Kāntipurī is rejected by modern historians.
b_kantit.etymology_analysis: Historic town and Gaharwar estate in Mirzapur district, Uttar Pradesh; no confirmed pre-867 CE attestation.

b_jaunpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded and named in 1359 CE by Delhi Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq in memory of his cousin Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Malik Jauna Khan).
b_jaunpur.eponym_details: Named after Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq (c. 1290–1351 CE, born Malik Jauna Khan) by his cousin Firuz Shah Tughlaq in 1359 CE.
b_jaunpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Jauna (from Malik Jauna Khan, Muhammad bin Tughlaq) + -pur ('city'), founded in 1359 CE.

b_gadhipuri.first_mention_attestation: Traditional/legendary Sanskrit name for Ghazipur (first mentioned in contemporary sources c. 1494 CE; founded per legend in 1330 CE); unattested in pre-867 CE sources.
b_gadhipuri.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Gādhipurī ('City of Gadhi'), a legendary pre-Islamic name attributed to Ghazipur in local tradition.

b_haldi2.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1484 CE during the Lodi–Sharqi War when Bahlul Lodi pursued Husain Shah Sharqi as far as Haldi in Ballia district.
b_haldi2.etymology_analysis: Historic village and Haihaya Rajput estate in Ballia district, Uttar Pradesh, attested from 1484 CE.

b_varanasi.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bārāṇasī in the early Buddhist Pāli Canon and as Vārāṇasī in Pāṇini and early Upaniṣads (c. 6th–5th century BCE); the region Kāśī appears in the Atharvaveda (c. 1000 BCE).
b_varanasi.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vārāṇasī, traditionally explained as the city situated between the Varuṇā and Asī tributaries of the Ganges.

b_bhadohi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in medieval and modern Uttar Pradesh administrative records.
b_bhadohi.etymology_analysis: City in eastern Uttar Pradesh, traditionally linked to the medieval Bhar rulers of the region; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_ayodhya.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ayodhyā in the Atharvaveda (10.2.31), Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa, and Gupta-period texts (which identify it with Sāketa of 5th-century BCE Buddhist texts).
b_ayodhya.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Ayodhyā ('unconquerable, not to be warred against'), ancient capital of Kosala on the Sarayu River.

b_faizabad.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1730 CE by Saadat Ali Khan I (Burhan-ul-Mulk), the first Nawab of Awadh, initially as a hunting lodge and cantonment called Bangla near Ayodhya, and expanded as the Awadhi capital named Faizabad under Safdar Jung and Shuja-ud-Daula.
b_faizabad.etymology_analysis: Perso-Arabic compound Faizabad ('Abode of Bounty/Grace'), founded c. 1730 CE by Nawab Saadat Ali Khan I on the Ghaghara (Sarayu) river beside Ayodhya.

b_gonda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in medieval and Mughal-era Awadh records.
b_gonda.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit-Hindi goṇḍa ('cattle-pen, cow-station'), or linked to ancient Gonarda; no pre-867 CE attestation for Gonda.

b_naimisa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Naimiṣa / Naimiṣāraṇya in the Mahābhārata (c. 4th century BCE–4th century CE) and the Purāṇas.

morphemes.translation: Naimisha (sacred forest, linked to nimiṣa 'twinkling of an eye')

b_naimisa.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Naimiṣa (Naimiṣāraṇya, modern Nimsar in Sitapur district), the sacred forest where the Mahābhārata was recited to assembled sages.

b_bahraich.first_mention_attestation: First prominently attested in 11th-century CE accounts of Ghazi Saiyyad Salar Masud (1033 CE) and later Mughal records.

morphemes.translation: Bahraich (traditionally linked to Brahmaich or Bhar tribe)

b_bahraich.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived either from Brahmāich ('assembly of Brahmā') or from the Bhar rulers of Awadh.

b_lakhimpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in modern Uttar Pradesh district records (Lakhimpur Kheri).
b_lakhimpur.etymology_analysis: Derived from Lakṣmīpur ('City of Lakshmi'); administrative headquarters of Lakhimpur Kheri district, Uttar Pradesh.

b_sravasti.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sāvatthī in the early Buddhist Pāli Canon (c. 5th century BCE) and as Śrāvastī in Pāṇini and the Rāmāyaṇa; visited by Faxian (c. 400 CE) and Xuanzang (c. 636 CE).

morphemes.translation: city of King Śrāvasta (or sage Sāvattha)

b_sravasti.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Śrāvastī (Pāli Sāvatthī), ancient capital of northern Kosala and major Buddhist center.

b_amorha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in early modern Basti/Awadh estate records (18th–19th centuries CE).
b_amorha.etymology_analysis: Historic village and former princely estate (Amorha Khas) in Basti district, Uttar Pradesh; unoccupied holding in repo.

b_gorakhpur.first_mention_attestation: Named after the medieval Nath yogi saint Gorakhnath (c. 11th–12th century CE); attested in medieval records thereafter.
b_gorakhpur.eponym_details: Named after the medieval Nath Hindu yogi saint Gorakhnath (c. 11th–12th century CE).
b_gorakhpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Gorakh(nāth) + -pur ('city'), named after the 11th–12th century CE Nath yogi Gorakhnath.

b_gurgi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 10th–11th century CE Kalachuri Gurgi inscription of Kokalla II / Yuvarājadeva.
b_gurgi.etymology_analysis: Archaeological site and Kalachuri religious center near Rewa, Madhya Pradesh, attested from the 10th–11th century CE Gurgi inscription.

b_chandrehi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Chandrehe stone inscription of Mattamayūra Shaiva leader Prabodhaśiva dated March 973 CE (Kalachuri year 724).
b_chandrehi.etymology_analysis: Historic Mattamayūra Shaiva monastery and temple site in Sidhi district, Madhya Pradesh, dated by its 973 CE inscription.

b_candhoba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE or standard historical gazetteer sources.
b_candhoba.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in northern Malwa (near Guna/Kadwaya); no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_guna.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; attested in modern Scindia/Gwalior State and Madhya Pradesh records (19th century CE).
b_guna.etymology_analysis: Town on the Parbati River in Madhya Pradesh, developed under the Scindia dynasty of Gwalior; no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_kadwaya.first_mention_attestation: Identified with medieval Kadambaguhā in an inscription dated c. 1000 CE; the modern name Kadwāhā/Kadwāyā is later.
b_kadwaya.etymology_analysis: Modern variant of Kadwāhā, identified with medieval Sanskrit Kadambaguhā ('Kadamba cave/grove'), a center of the Mattamayūra Shaiva sect.

b_chanderi.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 11th century CE under the Later Pratiharas (Kīrtipāla) and in al-Bīrūnī (1030 CE).

morphemes.translation: Chanderi (fortress town in Ashoknagar, linked to Chandragiri/Chedi)

b_chanderi.etymology_analysis: Historic fortress town in Madhya Pradesh settled and fortified in the 11th century CE by the Later Pratiharas.

b_jhansi.first_mention_attestation: Jhansi Fort was built on Bangra hill in 1613 CE by Raja Bir Singh Deo of Orchha; the surrounding settlement was initially called Balwantnagar before adopting the name Jhansi.
b_jhansi.etymology_analysis: Derived from a variant of Hindi jhāṛ ('bushes, undergrowth', from Sanskrit jhāṭa) with the reduced Sanskrit genitive suffix -sya (-sī), meaning 'covered in undergrowth'. Founded around Jhansi Fort in 1613 CE.

b_luacchagiri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE or dated historical records; appears only as a Sanskritized hill toponym in later medieval/Jain literary traditions.
b_luacchagiri.etymology_analysis: Compound ending in Sanskrit giri ('hill, mountain') with an obscure first element luaccha; lacks verifiable pre-867 CE epigraphic or textual attestation.

b_garh_kundar.first_mention_attestation: Fortress constructed between 925 and 940 CE by the Chandela ruler Yashovarman after conquering southwestern Bundelkhand.
b_garh_kundar.etymology_analysis: Named after the fort (gaṛh) of Kundar, derived from Sanskrit Kuṇḍārka (kuṇḍa 'pond' + arka 'sun'), referring to the sacred Arka-kund pond near the fort.

b_jarai_ka_math.first_mention_attestation: Although the red sandstone temple at Barua Sagar was built c. 860 CE under Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Mihira Bhoja, the vernacular Hindi name 'Jarai-ka-Math' is a modern designation unattested in 9th-century CE sources.
b_jarai_ka_math.etymology_analysis: Modern Hindi compound meaning 'shrine/monastery of Jarai', applied to the c. 860 CE Gurjara-Pratihara Devi temple near Barua Sagar.

b_sarangpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the mid-to-late 14th century CE (reign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq, 1351–1388 CE) by Shaikh Sarang, an amir of the Delhi Sultanate.
b_sarangpur.eponym_details: Named after Shaikh Sarang, a 14th-century CE amir of Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq who founded the town.
b_sarangpur.etymology_analysis: Eponymous compound combining the name of its 14th-century CE founder Shaikh Sarang with the Indic suffix -pur ('city, town').

b_ashta.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation of the name Ashta; the modern town was developed during the early modern/British period by Mirza Amjad Baig.
b_ashta.etymology_analysis: Town on the Parvati River in Sehore district; its name is unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphic or literary records.

b_gagraun.first_mention_attestation: Gagron Fort was constructed in the 12th century CE by Dod/Paramara ruler Bijaldev Singh Dod (with later medieval sieges in 1423 and 1444 CE).
b_gagraun.etymology_analysis: Hill-and-water fort (Jaladurg) at the confluence of the Ahu and Kali Sindh rivers, built in the 12th century CE; the name Gagraun/Gagron is unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_jhalawar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1791 CE as a cantonment (Chaoni Umedpura) by Jhala Zalim Singh, Dewan of Kota State.
b_jhalawar.eponym_details: Named after Jhala Zalim Singh (1730–1823 CE), the Jhala Rajput Dewan of Kota State who established the settlement in 1791 CE.
b_jhalawar.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Jhala clan name (after founder Jhala Zalim Singh) and -wāṛ ('enclosure, territory'), formed in the late 18th century CE.
