b_vidisa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Vedisa in a 1st-century BCE Brahmi inscription at Sanchi and associated with the ancient city of Besnagar (Heliodorus Pillar, c. 113 BCE) and Pali Buddhist texts.

morphemes.translation: name derived from the nearby Bais/Vais river

b_vidisa.etymology_analysis: Ancient Sanskrit toponym Vidiśā (Prakrit Vedisā), traditionally derived from the nearby Bais (Vais) river; capital of Dasharna and a major Mauryan-Shunga center.

b_raisin.first_mention_attestation: Raisen Fort was built in the 11th century CE on a hill overlooking the town.
b_raisin.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress town in Madhya Pradesh named after Rai Ka Mahal (11th century CE); unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_sironj.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1103 CE by Sengar Rajput warrior Shankar Singh as Sengar Raj, which later contracted to Sironj.
b_sironj.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Sengar Rāj ('rule of the Sengar Rajputs'), founded in 1103 CE by Shankar Singh Sengar.

b_sanchi.first_mention_attestation: The modern name Sanchi is post-867 CE; in antiquity the site was known as Chetiyagiri (Mahavamsa), Kakanaya (early Brahmi votive inscriptions), and Kakanada-bota (Gupta period).
b_sanchi.etymology_analysis: Modern name Sanchi is variously linked to Sanskrit/Pali sanch ('to measure') or Hindi sancha ('stone moulds'), replacing its ancient Buddhist names Kakanaya and Chetiyagiri.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Mauryan Ashoka Pillar and early Brahmi votive inscriptions (3rd–2nd century BCE); Gupta inscriptions (Kakanada-bota)
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Kakanaya in early votive inscriptions and Kakanada-bota in Gupta-era inscriptions.

b_bhojpur.first_mention_attestation: Named after Paramara King Bhoja (r. c. 1000–1055 CE); attested in an undated 11th-century Jain statue pedestal inscription mentioning Bhoja and a 1100 CE (VS 1157) inscription.
b_bhojpur.eponym_details: Named after King Bhoja of the Paramara dynasty (r. c. 1000–1055 CE), who built the Bhojeshwar temple and dams here.
b_bhojpur.etymology_analysis: Eponymous compound 'City of Bhoja', named after Paramara King Bhoja (r. c. 1000–1055 CE); no archaeological evidence predates the 11th century CE.

b_asirgarh.first_mention_attestation: Said to date to the late 14th or early 15th century CE (Firishta attributes it to Asa Ahir c. 1370 CE; Faruqi Sultan Nasir Khan captured it c. 1400 CE).
b_asirgarh.etymology_analysis: Compound of Asīr (either meaning 'impregnable height' or linked to the legendary Asa Ahir) and gaṛh ('fort'); unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_khandwa.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation of the town name Khandwa; medieval/modern name derived from Khandav Van.
b_khandwa.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Khāṇḍava-vana ('Khandava forest'); the modern settlement name Khandwa is unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_khargone.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation of Khargone; nearby Oon temples preserve 12th-century CE inscriptions (1165–1185 CE).
b_khargone.etymology_analysis: Town on the Kunda River in the Nimar region; unattested in pre-867 CE sources.

b_burhanpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1388 CE by Malik Nasir Khan of the Faruqi dynasty of Khandesh.
b_burhanpur.eponym_details: Named after the medieval Chishti Sufi saint Burhan-ud-Din Gharib (1256–1337 CE) when founded by Malik Nasir Khan in 1388 CE.
b_burhanpur.etymology_analysis: Eponymous compound 'City of Burhan', named in 1388 CE after Sufi saint Burhan-ud-Din Gharib.

b_erandol.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE historical attestation of Erandol; local tradition links the site to Ekachakra Nagari and Arunawati without contemporary epigraphic support.

morphemes.translation: Erandol (town name on the Anjani River)

b_erandol.etymology_analysis: Town on the Anjani River in Jalgaon district; unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE records.

b_changdev.first_mention_attestation: Named after the 13th–14th century CE yogi Changdev Maharaj (contemporary of Sant Dnyaneshwar and Muktabai, c. 1300 CE); earlier known as Sundarpur and Bhingnapur.
b_changdev.eponym_details: Named after yogi Changdev Maharaj (c. late 13th–early 14th century CE), who took samadhi at the site.
b_changdev.etymology_analysis: Named after the medieval Maharashtrian yogi Changdev Maharaj (c. 1300 CE); its earlier names Sundarpur and Bhingnapur are likewise unattested before 867 CE.

b_mandapika.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mandapa Durga in an inscription from Talanpur (Dhar district) dated Vikrama Samvat 612 (555 CE).
b_mandapika.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit maṇḍapa ('hall, pavilion'), attested in 555 CE as Mandapa Durga and later Prakritized as Mandava / Mandu.

b_bawangaja.first_mention_attestation: The monolithic Rishabhadeva statue dates to the early 12th century CE, and the Chulgiri temple carries inscriptions dated 1166 CE and 1459 CE.
b_bawangaja.etymology_analysis: Hindi compound meaning 'fifty-two yards', referring to the height of the 12th-century CE monolithic Jain statue of Rishabhadeva.

b_borgarh.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; refers to a regional fort/locality (Borgarh / Bhawargarh) in the Nimar–Malwa Satpura tract south of Dhar and the Narmada valley in Madhya Pradesh.

morphemes.translation: jujube/ber tree (or regional variant of bhawar)

b_borgarh.etymology_analysis: Indo-Aryan fort compound combining bor (Hindi/Malvi jujube tree or local variant) with garh ('fort'), denoting a hill fort/locality in western Madhya Pradesh.

b_thalner.first_mention_attestation: First capital of the Faruqi dynasty of Khandesh (late 14th century CE, c. 1382 CE); no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_thalner.etymology_analysis: Probably derived from the stone temple of Thaleshwar at the foot of the fort, combined with the regional settlement suffix -ner; rose to prominence as the first Faruqi capital in the late 14th century CE.

b_sindkheda.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; medieval settlement associated with the Rawals of Khandesh.
b_sindkheda.etymology_analysis: Marathi compound from śindī (wild date palm trees) and kheḍā ('village, settlement'), meaning 'village of palm trees'.

b_bhamer.first_mention_attestation: Medieval hill fort in Sakri tehsil; first explicitly dated documentary mention in a Peshwa letter of 10 July 1764 CE.
b_bhamer.etymology_analysis: Hill fort village in Dhule district associated with medieval Ahir/Gavali and Faruqi control; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_amalner.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in late 16th-century Mughal administrative and revenue rolls of Khandesh (Ain-i-Akbari, c. 1595 CE); unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources.
b_amalner.etymology_analysis: Historic town on the Bori River in Jalgaon district (Khandesh), Maharashtra, combining amal with the regional Maharashtrian settlement suffix -ner.

b_dhara.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Dhārā in the 6th-century CE Jaunpur stone inscription of the Maukhari dynasty (c. 554 CE).
b_dhara.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Dhārā Nagara ('city of sword blades'), attested in the 6th-century CE Maukhari inscription at Jaunpur and later the Paramara capital.

b_dharampuri.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a copper-plate charter issued in Vikrama Samvat 1031 (975 CE) by Paramara king Vakpati Munja, found at Dharampuri.
b_dharampuri.etymology_analysis: Compound from Sanskrit dharma ('righteousness, sacred duty') and purī ('town, city'), attested from 975 CE.

b_depalpur.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as a mahal of Ujjain sarkar in the Ain-i-Akbari (c. 1590 CE); although traditionally linked to Pala ruler Devapala (r. 810s–845 CE), no contemporary pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_depalpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Depāl (traditionally attributed to Devapala) and -pur ('town'); attested as a Mughal mahal in the Ain-i-Akbari (c. 1590 CE).

b_betma.first_mention_attestation: Listed as a mahal of Malwa in the Ain-i-Akbari (c. 1590 CE); a 1020 CE copper-plate of Bhoja was found here but records a different village (Nalatadaga).
b_betma.etymology_analysis: Locally linked to Hindi baiṭh-mā ('sit, mother'), attested as a Malwa pargana/mahal in the Ain-i-Akbari (c. 1590 CE).

b_dadhipadra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dadhipadra-mandala in the Dohad (Dahod) stone inscription of Chaulukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja dated Vikrama Samvat 1196 (1139–1140 CE).
b_dadhipadra.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit toponym Dadhipadra (from Sage Dadhichi or dadhi + padra 'village'), attested in the 1139–1140 CE Dohad inscription and evolved into modern Dahod.

b_champaner.first_mention_attestation: The c. 750 CE founding attribution to Vanaraja Chavda derives from later medieval Jain prabandhas (e.g., Merutunga's Prabandha Chintamani, 1304 CE); contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic or physical records at Champaner-Pavagadh are absent, with earliest surviving ruins dating to the 10th–11th centuries CE.
b_champaner.etymology_analysis: Named after Champa (Champaraj), general of 8th-century CE Chavda king Vanaraja, combined with the regional settlement suffix -ner.

b_ujjayini.first_mention_attestation: Emerged as the capital of Avanti Mahajanapada around 600 BCE (urbanized c. 700 BCE) and is attested in Buddhist texts and Ashokan edicts (3rd century BCE).
b_ujjayini.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Ujjayinī ('the victorious city', from ud- + jayinī), one of the seven sacred cities (Sapta Puri) and capital of ancient Avanti.

b_agar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 10th century CE by King Agria Bhil, who built the Baijnath Mahadev temple.
b_agar.eponym_details: Named after King Agria Bhil, who founded the town in the 10th century CE.
b_agar.etymology_analysis: Eponymous toponym named after 10th-century CE founder King Agria Bhil.

b_mehidpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; known in Mughal times as Muhammadpur and in modern history from the Battle of Mahidpur (20 December 1817 CE).
b_mehidpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Maheda (traditionally attributed to Raja Maheda Bhil) and -pur ('town'); unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_maksi.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation of the town name Maksi, though it houses a Svetambara Jain temple with a traditional ancient Parshvanatha idol.
b_maksi.etymology_analysis: Town in Shajapur district, Madhya Pradesh; the toponym Maksi lacks contemporary pre-867 CE attestation.

b_dewas.first_mention_attestation: Established as a sovereign Maratha territory in the first half of the 18th century CE (c. 1728 CE) by the Pawar brothers Tukoji Rao and Jivaji Rao.
b_dewas.etymology_analysis: Sandhi of deva ('deity') and vās ('abode'), meaning 'abode of the gods', derived from the Devi Vashini hill (Tekri) in the city.

b_dasapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Daśapura in 5th–6th century CE Aulikara inscriptions at Mandsaur (including the 436 CE silk-weavers guild inscription of Bandhuvarman and 532 CE Yashodharman inscription) and Kalidasa's Meghaduta.
b_dasapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound Daśapura ('ten cities/fortresses'), ancient name of Mandsaur attested in 5th-century CE Aulikara epigraphs.

b_dharmrajeshwar.first_mention_attestation: The rock-cut temple complex dates to the 8th century CE, but the modern name Dharmrajeshwar is not attested in contemporary pre-867 CE inscriptions.
b_dharmrajeshwar.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound Dharmarājeśvara ('Lord of Dharmaraja'), modern name of the 8th-century CE monolithic rock-cut Hindu shrine near Chandwasa.

b_vatapadraka.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Vatapadraka village in Vyaghradora bhoga of Sthali mandala (Vagada/Malwa border) in Paramara King Bhoja's Banswara copper-plate inscription dated 3 January 1020 CE.
b_vatapadraka.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound Vaṭapadraka ('banyan-tree village'), attested in the Malwa/Vagada region in Bhoja's 1020 CE Banswara copper-plate grant.

b_bannu.first_mention_attestation: Founded by the British in 1848 CE as Dhulipnagar, renamed Edwardesabad in 1869 CE, and officially named Bannu in 1903 CE; derives from ancient Avestan Varəna and Sanskrit Varṇu.

morphemes.translation: ancient name of the Bannu basin

b_bannu.etymology_analysis: Modern form Bannu (officially adopted in 1903 CE) is derived from Avestan Varəna and Sanskrit Varṇu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Panini's Ashtadhyayi (Varṇu, c. 5th century BCE) and Avestan Vendidad (Varəna)
older_name_by_867.notes: Michael Witzel identifies Avestan Varəna and Panini's Varṇu as the ancient predecessors of Bannu.

b_kalabagh.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; named in the early modern/medieval period after mango gardens planted by the Nawabs of Kalabagh.
b_kalabagh.etymology_analysis: Compound of kālā ('black') and bāgh ('garden'), referring to the dark-foliaged mango orchards planted by its Nawab founders.

b_hangu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; Aurel Stein noted a conjectural link to Chinese travelers, without contemporary attestation.
b_hangu.etymology_analysis: Town in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; Aurel Stein speculated a possible connection to Chinese travelers (comparing Chinese Hangu), but no pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_nandana.first_mention_attestation: Fortified settlement built by the Odi/Hindu Shahi dynasty (9th–11th centuries CE), attested in 1014 CE when captured by Mahmud of Ghazni and used by al-Biruni.
b_nandana.etymology_analysis: Sanskritic/Punjabi fortress name Nandana in the Salt Range, serving as the late Hindu Shahi capital after 1001 CE and falling in 1014 CE.

b_lund_nandana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; appears as a modern/medieval Punjabi-Potohari settlement name.
b_lund_nandana.etymology_analysis: Regional settlement name in northern Punjab/Salt Range; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_purushapura.first_mention_attestation: Became the eastern capital of the Kushan Empire under Kanishka (r. from 127 CE), attested on the Kanishka casket inscription and in Faxian (400 CE) and Xuanzang (634 CE).
b_purushapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Puruṣapura ('city of men'), the ancient capital of Gandhara under the Kushans from which modern Peshawar derives.

b_nowshera.first_mention_attestation: Developed during the Afghan Durrani Empire (18th century CE) and attested at the Battle of Nowshera in March 1823 CE.
b_nowshera.etymology_analysis: Persian/Urdu Nowshehra ('new city'), translating local Pashto Nowkhār ('new city').

b_shergarh.first_mention_attestation: Historic fort and town in Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, associated with the 16th-century Suri era of Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540–1545 CE); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_shergarh.eponym_details: Associated with the 16th-century Suri ruler Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540–1545 CE), after whom numerous Suri-era strongholds across northern India and the northwest frontier were named Shergarh.

morphemes.translation: lion; royal epithet of Sher Shah Suri

b_shergarh.etymology_analysis: Compound of Persian/Urdu sher ('lion', also the title of Sher Shah Suri) and Indo-Aryan garh ('fort'), denoting the historic stronghold/town in Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

b_udabhanda.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Udabhāṇḍapura (modern Hund), serving as the capital of Kapisa-Gandhara under the Turk Shahi dynasty from the 7th century CE.
b_udabhanda.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Udabhāṇḍapura ('city of water pots'), the Shahi capital on the Indus (modern Hund).

b_attak.first_mention_attestation: Established by Mughal Emperor Akbar in 1581–1583 CE as Atak-Banaras with the construction of Attock Fort.
b_attak.etymology_analysis: From Punjabi aṭak ('barrier, obstruction', or 'skirt of the mountains'), founded by Akbar in 1581 CE.

b_oddiyana.first_mention_attestation: Attested in a Kushan-era inscription mentioning the monk Jivaka Odiyanaka (2nd century CE), and in Faxian (c. 400 CE) and Xuanzang (7th century CE).
b_oddiyana.etymology_analysis: Middle Indic/Prakrit form of Sanskrit Udyāna ('garden, orchard'), the historical region centered on the Swat Valley.

b_mankiala.first_mention_attestation: While the Manikyala Stupa dates to the reign of Kanishka (128–151 CE, Kharoshthi inscription year 18), the modern village name Mankiala is unattested in pre-867 CE sources.
b_mankiala.etymology_analysis: Modern village name near the 2nd-century CE Manikyala Stupa; the toponym itself lacks contemporary pre-867 CE attestation.

b_urgun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical or epigraphic sources.
b_urgun.etymology_analysis: Town in Paktika Province, Afghanistan; lacks pre-867 CE attestation.

b_shakin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical or epigraphic sources.
b_shakin.etymology_analysis: Modern settlement/district name (Shkin/Shakin) in Paktika Province, Afghanistan; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_khost.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical or epigraphic sources.
b_khost.etymology_analysis: Name of the Khost valley and city in eastern Afghanistan; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_bhera.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Ghaznavid campaigns under Mahmud of Ghazni in the early 11th century CE (c. 1004 CE).
b_bhera.etymology_analysis: Ancient town on the Jhelum River, first recorded by name in 11th-century CE Ghaznavid sources (and rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri in 1540 CE).

b_katasraj.first_mention_attestation: Although the oldest temple (Satghara Temple B) dates to the late 6th century CE and Xuanzang visited the springs in the 7th century CE, the modern name Katas Raj is unattested <= 867 CE.
b_katasraj.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit kaṭākṣa ('tearful eyes', referring to the sacred pond Katakshkund) + rāj; modern name unattested before 867 CE.

b_phalia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; modern town in Mandi Bahauddin District, though local tradition links the area to Alexander's Bucephala.
b_phalia.etymology_analysis: Town in Punjab, Pakistan; the name Phalia is unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_gurjaratra.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Gurjaratrā in the Ghatiyala inscription of the Mandavyapura Pratihara ruler Kakkuka in 861 CE.
b_gurjaratra.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Gurjaratrā ('country of the Gurjaras'), attested in 861 CE in the Ghatiyala inscription (and applied in Punjab to the Gujrat/Alakhana kingdom in the 9th century CE).

b_jhelum.first_mention_attestation: The modern name Jhelum is post-867 CE; in antiquity, Alexander founded Bucephala nearby on the Hydaspes (Jhelum) River in 326 BCE.
b_jhelum.etymology_analysis: Popularly derived from jal ('pure water') and ham ('snow'), referring to the Himalayan-fed river; the modern name Jhelum is post-867 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian (Anabasis Alexandri, recording Alexander's 326 BCE foundation after the Battle of the Hydaspes)
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Greek accounts place Bucephala near modern Jhelum on the Hydaspes River.

b_kunjah.first_mention_attestation: Grew in prominence in the 9th–10th centuries CE and is documented as a military base under Ghaznavid Sultan Ibrahim ibn Mas'ud (r. 1059–1099 CE).
b_kunjah.etymology_analysis: Traditionally named after a Raja Kunjpal; documented in the Ghaznavid period (11th century CE) with no contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kangra.first_mention_attestation: The modern name Kangra (and medieval Nagarkot/Bhimanagar) is post-867 CE; the region and stronghold were known in antiquity as Trigarta.
b_kangra.etymology_analysis: Linked to the Himalayan word kangri ('snow on mountain peak'), replacing the ancient regional name Trigarta.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Panini's Ashtadhyayi (c. 5th century BCE) and Mahabharata
older_name_by_867.notes: Historically known as Trigarta (and Kiraj) prior to Nagarkot/Kangra.

b_brahmapura.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 500 CE by Raja Maru and attested in late Gupta-script inscriptions of Meruvarman (c. 700 CE) at the Lakshana Devi temple in Bharmour.
b_brahmapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Brahmapura ('city of Brahma'), the ancient capital of Chamba state (modern Bharmour), attested c. 700 CE.

b_campa2.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 920 CE by Raja Sahila Varman of Brahmapura, who named the new capital Champavati/Champa.
b_campa2.eponym_details: Named after Champavati, daughter of Raja Sahila Varman, who founded the town around 920 CE.
b_campa2.etymology_analysis: Shortened from Champavati, named c. 920 CE after Raja Sahila Varman's daughter Champavati (modern Chamba).

b_lahur.first_mention_attestation: First documented by name in the Persian geographical treatise Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE).
b_lahur.etymology_analysis: Early Muslim form (Luhāwar, Lūhār, Lāhūr) first attested in 982 CE; scholars suggest derivation either from Ravāwar (< Iravatyāwar, after the Ravi River) or Lohār ('blacksmith').

b_kasur.first_mention_attestation: Established as a fortified town in 1525 CE by the Kheshgi tribe of Pashtuns during the reign of Babur.
b_kasur.etymology_analysis: From Arabic/Persian quṣūr ('palaces, forts'), reflecting the twelve fortified hamlets (kots) established by the Kheshgi Afghans in 1525 CE.

b_sangla.first_mention_attestation: The modern name Sangla Hill is post-867 CE and unattested in pre-867 CE sources.

morphemes.translation: Sangla (town name in Nankana Sahib district)

b_sangla.etymology_analysis: Modern Punjabi town (Sangla Hill) in Nankana Sahib district; unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_chunian.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary sources by 867 CE; the present town is over 500 years old (late medieval/Mughal era), though built on an older archaeological mound yielding coins from c. 323 BCE.
b_chunian.eponym_details: Popularly attributed to Chunni, daughter of Raja Todar Mal (16th century CE), revenue minister to Mughal emperor Akbar.

morphemes.translation: personal name (daughter of Raja Todar Mal)

b_chunian.etymology_analysis: Locally derived in folk tradition from Chunni, daughter of 16th-century Mughal minister Raja Todar Mal, with a Punjabi associative/plural suffix (-an). While archaeological mounds at the site show ancient occupation, the toponym Chunian is not attested by 867 CE.

b_sakala.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sangala (Ancient Greek: Σάγγαλα) in Arrian's Anabasis of Alexander for Alexander the Great's 326 BCE campaign, and as Śākala in the Sanskrit Mahabharata and the Buddhist Milinda Panha.

morphemes.translation: ancient capital of the Madra kingdom (modern Sialkot)

b_sakala.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Śākala (Pali Sāgala, Greek Σάγγαλα), the ancient capital of the Madra kingdom in Punjab, later capital of the Indo-Greek king Menander I (2nd century BCE) and the Alchon Hun ruler Mihirakula (6th century CE), corresponding to modern Sialkot.

b_jammu.first_mention_attestation: Attested around 900 CE in the Tarikh-i-Azmi; local tradition attributes its founding to Raja Jambulochan in the 9th century CE, though contemporary pre-867 written attestation is lacking.

morphemes.translation: legendary founder Raja Jambulochan (or rose-apple tree)

b_jammu.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Raja Jambulochan, a semi-legendary 9th-century founder, or Sanskrit jambu (rose-apple). The region was known as Durgara from c. 900 CE, and Jammu itself is not contemporarily attested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_bhuttar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; named after the Punjabi Jat/Rajput clan Buttar/Bhutta.
b_bhuttar.etymology_analysis: Settlement name derived from the Buttar (or Bhutta) Jat clan of Punjab, prevalent in Sialkot and central Punjab. No contemporary written attestation exists by 867 CE.

b_bhirr.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a proper settlement name by 867 CE; Punjabi/Saraiki bhirr ('ruined mound') denotes the ancient archaeological mound adjacent to Shorkot in Jhang district, Punjab, Pakistan.
b_bhirr.etymology_analysis: From Punjabi/Saraiki bhir / bhirr ('ruined mound'), referring locally to the towering ancient tell of Shorkot in Jhang district, Punjab, Pakistan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Shorkot copper-pot inscription dated Gupta Samvat 83 (403 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The Shorkot Bhirr archaeological mound is identified epigraphically with ancient Śivipura (Sibipura), attested in 403 CE.

b_shorkot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the name Shorkot by 867 CE; the ancient mound of Shorkot in Jhang district, Punjab, Pakistan was attested in 403 CE under the earlier name Śivipura (Sibipura).

morphemes.translation: vernacular reflex of Śivipura or legendary local name

b_shorkot.etymology_analysis: Compound of Punjabi/Indo-Aryan kot ('fort') and Shor, likely a vernacular evolution of ancient Śivipura (Sibipura); although the mound is ancient, the name Shorkot is not attested by 867 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Shorkot copper-pot inscription dated Samvat 83 (Gupta era, 403 CE), recording a donation to Sarvastivada Buddhists at Śivipura.
older_name_by_867.notes: Identified archaeologically and epigraphically with the ancient Shorkot mound.

b_kamalia.first_mention_attestation: The modern settlement of Kamalia was founded in the 14th century CE by Kamal Khan, a chief of the Kharal tribe; Alexander Cunningham identified the nearby ancient mound with a Mallian town of 325 BCE.
b_kamalia.eponym_details: Named after Kamal Khan (Kot Kamal -> Kamalia), a 14th-century CE chief of the Kharal tribe.
b_kamalia.etymology_analysis: Derived from Kot Kamal ('Fort of Kamal'), named after the 14th-century CE Kharal chieftain Kamal Khan. Although the site has ancient Mallian-era remains, the name Kamalia dates to the 14th century CE.

b_jalandhar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the kingdom and city of Jalandhara in the Mahabharata and Puranas, and explicitly visited and documented by Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang c. 635 CE (as She-lan-ta-lo); earlier classical geography (Ptolemy, c. 150 CE) also describes the adjacent Kulindrine region.

morphemes.translation: holding, bearer (also linked to the Puranic asura Jalandhara)

b_jalandhar.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Jalandhara ('Water-bearing tract' between the Sutlej and Beas rivers, also mythologized in the Padma Purana via the demon Jalandhara), an ancient urban center and kingdom of Punjab.

b_rahon.first_mention_attestation: Local tradition records that Rahon was called Raghupur until the 12th century CE, when Raj Pal renamed it Rahon after a lady named Raho; earliest historical records include the 1710 CE Battle of Rahon.
b_rahon.eponym_details: Traditionally renamed in the 12th century CE by Raj Pal from Raghupur to Rahon after a lady named Raho.
b_rahon.etymology_analysis: According to local tradition, renamed from Raghupur to Rahon in the 12th century CE by Raj Pal in honor of a lady named Raho. Neither Rahon nor Raghupur has contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_pathankot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the modern compound name Pathankot by 867 CE; the medieval fortification name evolved from ancient Paithan (Pratishthana), an Audumbara urban and minting center attested on coins from c. 2nd–1st century BCE.
b_pathankot.etymology_analysis: Medieval contraction of Paithan-kot ('Fort of Paithan'), derived from ancient Sanskrit Pratishthana (giving rise to the Pathania clan name) plus Indo-Aryan kot ('fort').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Audumbara coinage (c. 2nd–1st century BCE) and ancient Sanskrit geographical tradition
older_name_by_867.notes: Pathankot was historically known as Pratishthana (Prakrit Paithan), an important Audumbara center prior to the later medieval addition of -kot.

b_kahlur.first_mention_attestation: Although the state was traditionally founded c. 697 CE by Raja Bir Chand, it was named Kahlur only after Raja Kahal Chand (r. 890–930 CE) built Kahlur Fort.
b_kahlur.eponym_details: Named after Raja Kahal Chand (r. 890–930 CE), who built Kahlur Fort (Kahal-pur -> Kahlur).
b_kahlur.etymology_analysis: Derived from Kahal-pur (contracted to Kahlur), named after Raja Kahal Chand (reigned 890–930 CE) who constructed Kahlur Fort. Because Kahal Chand ruled after 867 CE, the name Kahlur is post-867.

b_kafirkot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the name Kafirkot by 867 CE; the Hindu Shahi temple complex dates to c. 7th–10th century CE, while the Perso-Arabic exonym 'Kafir Kot' ('Fort of the Infidels') arose after the 11th-century Ghaznavid conquest.
b_kafirkot.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Perso-Arabic and Indo-Aryan compound meaning 'Fort of the Infidels', applied in the Islamic era (post-11th century CE) to the ruined Hindu Shahi temple-fortress complex in Dera Ismail Khan.

b_dera_ghazi_khan.first_mention_attestation: Founded at the end of the 15th century CE by the Dodai Baloch chieftain Ghazi Khan, son of Haji Khan Mirani.
b_dera_ghazi_khan.eponym_details: Named after Dodai Baloch chieftain Ghazi Khan Mirani, who founded the settlement in the late 15th century CE.
b_dera_ghazi_khan.etymology_analysis: Saraiki ḍerā ('tent, encampment, settlement') combined with the name of its late 15th-century founder, Ghazi Khan Mirani.

b_daraban.first_mention_attestation: First documented in British colonial records by Herbert Benjamin Edwardes in 1848–1849 CE as 'Daraban' or 'Drabund'.
b_daraban.etymology_analysis: According to H. B. Edwardes (1848–1849 CE), derived from Persian/Pashto darah-band ('closed pass'), referring to its position at the foot of the Sulaiman Mountains. Unattested by 867 CE.

b_loralai.first_mention_attestation: Established as a British military garrison and administrative town in 1886 CE (with Loralai District formed in 1903 CE), named after the Loralai (Lora) River in northeastern Balochistan, Pakistan.
b_loralai.etymology_analysis: Directly adopts the Pashto hydronym of the Loralai River (from Pashto lora, 'mountain stream/torrent') in the Bori Valley of Balochistan.

b_kohlu.first_mention_attestation: Earliest documented administrative mention in 1892 CE when a British sub-tehsil was established at Kohlu.
b_kohlu.etymology_analysis: Balochi/Persian toponym likely derived from koh ('mountain/hill'), reflecting its location in the Marri-Bugti hills of Balochistan. No pre-19th-century written attestation exists.

b_mekhtar.first_mention_attestation: Earliest documented mention in 1886 CE in British colonial military records for Loralai District (stationing of a military post at Mekhtar).
b_mekhtar.etymology_analysis: Likely related to Persian/Pashto mehtar ('chief, elder'). Oral tradition of the Khajjak Pashtuns places them in the Mekhtar area prior to c. 1700 CE, with written attestation beginning in 1886 CE.

b_zhob.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the town was established as Fort Sandeman in the British colonial period and renamed Zhob (after the Zhob River) in 1976 CE.
b_zhob.etymology_analysis: From Pashto ẓ̌ob ('oozing water'), the name of the Zhob River, which was adopted for the city in 1976 CE (previously Fort Sandeman). Neither the river nor the settlement has written attestation by 867 CE.

b_karor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the 1883 Punjab Gazetteer dates the tiled tombs at Karor Lal Esan (Kot Karor) to the 15th or 16th century CE.
b_karor.etymology_analysis: Known historically as Kot Karor and later Karor Lal Esan (after the 15th/16th-century Sufi saint Lal Esan). Unlike Kahror Pacca near Multan, Karor in Layyah has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_mankera.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the name Mankera by 867 CE; local tradition attributes an earlier fortress Mal Khir Kot to Raja Mal Khira in 540 CE, while Mankera Fort itself is documented from 1380 CE and 1804 CE.
b_mankera.etymology_analysis: Traditionally evolved from Mal Khir Kot (attributed in local lore to Raja Mal Khira of the Mal tribe in 540 CE) to Mankera. Contemporary pre-867 written attestation is absent.

b_wan_bhachran.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; associated with a well (wan) constructed by Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540–1545 CE) and the local Bhachar Awan clan.
b_wan_bhachran.etymology_analysis: Punjabi compound of wān ('well', referring to a 16th-century well built by Sher Shah Suri) and Bhachrān (the Bhachar clan of the Qutabshahi Awans).

b_karur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Karur (modern Kahror Pacca) in the Chachnama's account of Muhammad bin Qasim's 712 CE conquest of Multan, where Akrama ibn Rihan Shami was appointed governor of the forts of Ajtahad and Karur.
b_karur.etymology_analysis: Ancient fortified town (modern Kahror Pacca in Lodhran District) attested in the 8th-century Arabic conquest narrative preserved in the Chachnama (712 CE) and later by Al-Biruni (11th century CE).

b_askhanda.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Askalanda (Askhanda) in the Chachnama's account of Muhammad bin Qasim's 712 CE campaign toward Multan after crossing the Beas.

morphemes.translation: fortified stronghold between the Beas and Multan (possibly Alexander/Skanda-derived)

b_askhanda.etymology_analysis: Recorded as the stronghold of Askalanda in the 8th-century Arabic conquest account of Muhammad bin Qasim (712 CE) preserved in the Chachnama; sometimes linked by scholars to Iskandariya (Alexandria) or Skanda.

b_vehari.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; situated along the 16th-century Multan–Delhi Road built by Sher Shah Suri, and Vehari District was formed in 1976 CE.
b_vehari.etymology_analysis: Punjabi toponym (also spelled Vihari), possibly from Sanskrit/Prakrit vihāra ('dwelling, monastery') or a local clan/caravanserai name along the Multan–Delhi route. No written attestation exists by 867 CE.

b_multan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mu-lo-san-pu-lu (Mūlasthānapura) by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang in 641 CE, and as Multān in Arab accounts of the 712 CE conquest and Merchant Sulaiman (851 CE).
b_multan.etymology_analysis: Generally derived from Sanskrit Mūlasthāna ('original/root place', attested via Xuanzang's 641 CE Mūlasthānapura), or alternatively from Malli-stān (after the ancient Malli people) or Old Persian mulastāna ('frontier land').

b_kabirwala.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 16th century CE and named after the Sufi saint Baba Pir Kabir; attested in British colonial records as a tehsil of Multan District.
b_kabirwala.eponym_details: Named after the 16th-century CE Sufi saint Baba Pir Kabir (Hazrat Kabiruddin).
b_kabirwala.etymology_analysis: Punjabi compound of the personal name Kabīr (Baba Pir Kabir, 16th century CE) and the possessive/toponymic suffix -wālā ('place of').

b_tulamba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the name Tulamba by 867 CE; while archaeological excavations show habitation over 2,500 years old (Hindu, Buddhist, and Islamic layers), the modern name Tulamba is not documented in pre-867 written sources.

morphemes.translation: ancient mound/town on the Ravi River

b_tulamba.etymology_analysis: Ancient settlement on the eastern bank of the Ravi River with archaeological strata spanning over two millennia, though the toponym Tulamba itself lacks contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_alipur.first_mention_attestation: Documented as a Panwar Rajput state until 1701 CE, after which it passed to the Nawabs of Muzaffargarh.
b_alipur.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Arabic-Indo-Aryan toponym meaning 'Town of Ali', attested only in the early modern period (until 1701 CE under Panwar Rajputs).

b_uch.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the name Uch by 867 CE; early Muslim historians recorded the town as Bhatia (1006 CE) until the 12th century CE, with the name Uch emerging from the 12th–13th century CE.
b_uch.etymology_analysis: From Punjabi/Indo-Aryan ūch ('high', cf. Sanskrit ucca), or in local legend from a princess named Ucha Rani. Until the 12th century CE it was known as Bhatia, and Alexander Cunningham identified the ancient site with Alexandria on the Indus (325 BCE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian's Anabasis of Alexander (325 BCE foundation at the Indus–Acesines confluence, identified with Uch by Alexander Cunningham).
older_name_by_867.notes: Uch was later called Bhatia (1006 CE) before adopting the name Uch in the 12th century CE.

b_derawar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; later Bhati Rajput chronicles attribute the fort's initial construction (as Dera Rawal) to Rai Jajja Bhati in 858 CE, later renovated in 1732 CE.
b_derawar.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Dera Rawal / Dera Rawar ('Abode/Fort of the Rawal'), traditionally built by Rai Jajja Bhati as a tribute to Rawal Deoraj Bhati. Because the 858 CE date rests on later bardic tradition rather than contemporary <= 867 CE records, it is not contemporarily attested.

b_chachran.first_mention_attestation: Earliest documented mention in the Indian Postal Guide of 1875 CE; associated with the 19th-century Punjabi poet-saint Khawaja Ghulam Farid (b. 1845 CE).
b_chachran.etymology_analysis: Saraiki/Punjabi toponym (Chāchrāṅ Sharīf), likely from a local clan name with the associative suffix -ān. First documented in 19th-century colonial postal records.

b_pancapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Pancapura (Panchapura / Panchapattana, identified by historians with the Sutlej–Beas frontier post at Dipalpur/Panjpur in Punjab) in 12th-century Chahamana inscriptions recording Kilhana's campaign under Prithviraja II (c. 1168 CE).
b_pancapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Pancapura ('Five Towns', also Panchapattana / vernacular Panjpur), attested in 12th-century Chahamana records for the strategic Punjab frontier town.

b_dipalpur.first_mention_attestation: First concretely documented under the name Dipalpur in Delhi Sultanate chronicles of the late 13th century CE (notably Balban's and Prince Muhammad's 1285 CE frontier defense against the Mongols); although built on a Kushan-era mound and traditionally attributed to Raja Deva Pala, no pre-867 CE written attestations survive.

morphemes.translation: traditional founder name Raja Deva Pala

b_dipalpur.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Sanskrit/Punjabi Deva-pala-pura ('City of Raja Deva Pala'), denoting the historic fortified frontier city of Depalpur in Okara district, Punjab, Pakistan.

b_ajodhan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 13th century CE when Sufi saint Baba Farid (1173–1266 CE) established his jama khana at Ajodhan, and later in the Ain-i-Akbari (16th century CE); renamed Pakpattan in the 16th century CE.
b_ajodhan.etymology_analysis: Pre-16th-century Hindu name of Pakpattan, interpreted from Sanskrit Aja-dhana ('eternal wealth'), or alternatively associated with the ancient Yaudheya/Ayodhana tribe. Contemporary written attestation by 867 CE is lacking.

b_abohar.first_mention_attestation: Dates back to the 12th century CE in local tradition (founded by Abheraj Bhatti as Abhegarh) and is attested in the 14th century CE via Tughluq-era sources (Shams-i Siraj 'Afif) and the 16th-century Ain-i-Akbari.
b_abohar.eponym_details: Traditionally founded in the 12th century CE by Abheraj Bhatti (Abhegarh -> Abohar).
b_abohar.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Abhegarh, founded by the 12th-century Bhatti Rajput ruler Abheraj Bhatti. Attested in Delhi Sultanate and Mughal sources from the 14th century CE onward.

b_satghara.first_mention_attestation: Associated with the 16th-century CE Baloch leader Mir Chakar Rind (tomb at Satghara), though Kushan-era coins have been found in the surrounding mound.
b_satghara.etymology_analysis: Punjabi compound of sat ('seven') and gharā ('houses' or 'pitchers'), conventionally linked to the seven-house settlement of Mir Chakar Rind in the 16th century CE.

b_shakambhari.first_mention_attestation: Earliest surviving contemporary epigraphic record of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari (modern Sambhar, Rajasthan) is the 973 CE Harsha stone inscription of Vigraharaja II, which traces the dynasty back to Guvaka I in the early 9th century CE (while the 1170 CE Bijolia inscription traces Vasudeva to the 6th–7th century CE).
b_shakambhari.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Shakambhari ('Herb-bearing' tutelary goddess of the Chahamanas), naming the Chahamana capital at modern Sambhar Salt Lake in Rajasthan.

b_pushkar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Sanchi inscriptions from the 2nd century BCE, punch-marked coins (4th–2nd century BCE), and the Sanskrit Ramayana and Mahabharata.
b_pushkar.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit puṣkara ('blue lotus'), referring to the sacred lake and pilgrimage town where, in Hindu tradition, Brahma dropped a lotus flower. Attested in Sanchi inscriptions from the 2nd century BCE and in the Sanskrit epics.

b_ajayameru.first_mention_attestation: Earliest attested mention of Ajayameru (modern Ajmer) occurs in Palha's Pattavali copied in 1113 CE (1170 VS) at Dhara, and in Vigraharaja IV's Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra prashasti crediting Chahamana king Ajayaraja II with its founding.
b_ajayameru.eponym_details: Named after Chahamana ruler Ajayaraja II (early 12th century CE; 'Invincible Hill of Ajaya').

morphemes.translation: invincible; personal name of king Ajayaraja

b_ajayameru.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Ajaya-meru ('Invincible Hill' or 'Hill of Ajaya'), founded by Chahamana king Ajayaraja II in the early 12th century CE on Taragarh Hill and later contracted to Ajmer.

b_dhanop.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; a village in Bhilwara district known for the Dhanop Mata (Sheetla Mata) temple.
b_dhanop.etymology_analysis: Rajasthani village name in Bhilwara district associated with the Dhanop Mataji shrine. No contemporary pre-867 written attestation exists.

b_gwalior.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the vernacularized name Gwalior by 867 CE; contemporary Sanskrit inscriptions from 525 CE through 876 CE record the site as Gopagiri or Gopādri.
b_gwalior.etymology_analysis: Modern vernacular evolution of Sanskrit Gopagiri ('Cowherd Hill', attested in 6th–9th century CE inscriptions), or in popular legend named after the sage Gwalipa who cured Suraj Sen.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Gwalior stone inscription of the Alchon Hun ruler Mihirakula (c. 525 CE) and the 876 CE Chaturbhuja Temple inscription.
older_name_by_867.notes: Gwalior is the later medieval vernacular form of Sanskrit Gopagiri/Gopādri.

b_dabra.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; modern town and municipality in Gwalior district, Madhya Pradesh.
b_dabra.etymology_analysis: Hindi/Bundeli toponym ḍabrā ('pond, depression, marshy ground'). No contemporary written attestation exists by 867 CE.

b_narwar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Nalapura in medieval Sanskrit inscriptions from the 12th–13th centuries CE (e.g., the 1281 CE Bangla/Narwar inscriptions of the Yajvapalas and the 1288 CE Balvan inscription).
b_narwar.etymology_analysis: Vernacular contraction of Sanskrit Nalapura ('City of King Nala'), attested in medieval Sanskrit inscriptions from the 12th century CE onward.

b_sabalgarh.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 17th century CE by Gurjar sardar Sabal Singh, a noble in the court of the rulers of Karauli.
b_sabalgarh.eponym_details: Named after 17th-century CE Gurjar chieftain Sabal Singh Gujjar, who founded the town and fort.
b_sabalgarh.etymology_analysis: Compound of the personal name Sabal (Sabal Singh Gujjar, 17th century CE) and Hindi gaṛh ('fort').

b_ranthambore.first_mention_attestation: Founded during the mid-10th century CE (c. 944 CE) by Chauhan ruler Sapaldaksha (or Ranthambhan Dev).
b_ranthambore.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Raṇastambhapura ('City of the Pillar of Battle', contracted to Ranthambore), a hill fort founded by the Chahamanas in the mid-10th century CE.

b_mandrael.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1327 CE when Jadaun Raja Arjun Dev captured Mandrayal Fort, and in 1504 CE when Sultan Sikandar Lodi captured Mandrayal.

morphemes.translation: hill fort name on the Chambal

b_mandrael.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress town (Mandrayal/Mandrael) in Karauli district overlooking the Chambal River, attested from the 14th century CE onward.

b_gangapur.first_mention_attestation: Established in the 18th century CE (originally named Kushalgarh by Kushaliram Haldiya) and renamed Gangapur after his brother Gangaram.
b_gangapur.eponym_details: Named after Gangaram (18th century CE), brother of Kushaliram Haldiya.
b_gangapur.etymology_analysis: Compound of the personal name Gangaram (18th century CE) and Sanskrit/Hindi -pur ('town').

b_sheopur.first_mention_attestation: Earliest attested reference is a Jain pillar edict dated 1026 CE mentioning Sheopur Fort; the town was later refounded/fortified by Gaur Rajputs in 1537/1573 CE.
b_sheopur.etymology_analysis: Derived from Seep-pur ('town on the Seep River', contracted to Sheopur), or associated with Lord Shiva worshipped by the Gaur Rajputs. First attested in a 1026 CE Jain pillar inscription.

b_sakarai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Sakarai (Sakrai) Stone Inscription dated Vikrama Samvat 699 (642 CE per B. Ch. Chhabra in Epigraphia Indica Vol. XXVII; alternately read as VS 749 / 692 CE by G. H. Ojha or VS 879 / 822 CE by D. R. Bhandarkar—all <= 867 CE).
b_sakarai.etymology_analysis: Toponym in Sikar district (Shekhawati, Rajasthan) associated with the Sakrai Mata temple, contemporarily attested by the Sakrai Stone Inscription of Vikrama Samvat 699 (642 CE).

b_khaluvana.first_mention_attestation: Attested only in medieval/post-867 Chauhan-era records (listed as 'Khaluvana village in the Chandel pargana' in Dasharatha Sharma's Early Chauhan Dynasties).
b_khaluvana.etymology_analysis: Medieval village in Rajasthan (Chandel pargana) referenced in Chauhan-period epigraphic studies, lacking contemporary attestation by 867 CE.

b_harshnath.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 973 CE (VS 1030) Harsha stone inscription of Chahamana king Vigraharaja II, recording grants to the Shiva (Harshnath) temple on Mount Harsha in Sikar district, Rajasthan.

morphemes.translation: joy, delight (name of the hill and Shiva epithet)

b_harshnath.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Harshanatha ('Lord of Joy'), referring to Lord Shiva as the tutelary deity (kuladevata) of the Shakambhari Chahamanas enshrined atop Harshagiri hill near Sikar.

b_vairata.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Viratanagara (Vairata / Bairat) in the 6th–5th century BCE Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya and Mahabharata (as capital of Matsya Mahajanapada), in Ashoka's Bairat and Bhabru rock edicts (c. 250 BCE), and in Xuanzang's 634 CE travel account.

morphemes.translation: King Virata of the Matsya kingdom

b_vairata.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vairata (derived from Viratanagara, modern Bairat / Viratnagar in Rajasthan), the ancient capital of the Matsya kingdom attested in early Buddhist texts, Mauryan Ashokan edicts, and Xuanzang's travels.

b_sanganer.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the early 16th century CE by Kachwaha Rajput prince Sangaji (or associated with Rana Sanga); famous for 16th–17th-century block printing.
b_sanganer.eponym_details: Named after Kachwaha Rajput prince Sangaji (early 16th century CE).
b_sanganer.etymology_analysis: Rajasthani compound of the personal name Sāṅgā (early 16th-century Kachwaha prince Sangaji) and -ner (from Sanskrit nagara, 'town').

b_amer.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by Kachwaha ruler Raja Kakil Dev in 1037 CE (originally a Meena settlement named Ambikeshwar); became the Kachwaha capital of Dhundhar around 1207 CE.
b_amer.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Ambikeshwar (or Ambavati/Amba), originally a Meena settlement conquered by the Kachwahas in 1037 CE. Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE.

b_reni.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 942 CE (with a Jain temple built in 942 CE) and in Bikaner state records as Reni nizamat; renamed Taranagar in 1948 CE.

morphemes.translation: traditional name (attributed to a woman named Rinkali)

b_reni.etymology_analysis: Historic town in Churu district (modern Taranagar), formerly called Reni, traditionally named after a woman named Rinkali. Earliest dated monument is a 942 CE Jain temple; unattested by 867 CE.

b_dadrewa.first_mention_attestation: Associated with the 11th-century CE Chauhan warrior-saint Gogaji (born at Dadrewa), with literary attestation in the 16th-century Gogaji ra Rasawvala.
b_dadrewa.etymology_analysis: Historic Chauhan village in Churu district, Rajasthan, celebrated as the 11th-century CE birthplace of folk deity Gogaji. No contemporary attestation exists by 867 CE.

b_vikramapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bikampur (Vikramapura) in 15th-century Marwar/Bikaner chronicles (occupied by Rao Ranmal c. 1420s CE and granted as a jagir by Rao Bika in 1482 CE).
b_vikramapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized form of Bikampur ('City of Vikrama/Bikam'), a medieval Bhati and Rathore stronghold in the Bikaner/Jaisalmer desert tract attested from the 15th century CE.

b_kolayat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; a traditional pilgrimage site associated with the Vedic sage Kapila (Kapilayatana -> Kolayat).
b_kolayat.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Sanskrit Kapilāyatana ('Abode/Sanctuary of Sage Kapila') to Kolayat. Despite its mythological association with Kapila, contemporary written attestation by 867 CE is lacking.

b_candravati.first_mention_attestation: Flourished from the 10th to 13th centuries CE as the capital of the Paramaras of Mount Abu (Sirohi district, Rajasthan), with dated stone inscriptions of the Chandravati Paramara lineage surviving from the 11th century CE (e.g., Purnapala's 1042 CE inscription).
b_candravati.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Chandravati ('Moonlit / Endowed with the Moon'), the medieval Paramara capital on the West Banas River near Mount Abu in southern Rajasthan.

b_bhillamala.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Pi-lo-mo-lo (Bhillamāla) by Xuanzang (631–645 CE) as the capital of Gurjara-desa, and as the birthplace of mathematician Brahmagupta (fl. 628 CE).
b_bhillamala.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Bhillamāla (modern Bhinmal, also called Śrīmāla), meaning 'Tract/Garland of the Bhils', attested in the 7th century CE by Xuanzang and in the works of Brahmagupta.

b_jalor.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jābālipura in Uddyotana-sūri's Prakrit romance Kuvalayamālā, composed at Jabalipura (Jalore) in 779 CE during the reign of Gurjara-Pratihara king Vatsaraja.
b_jalor.etymology_analysis: Vernacular contraction of Sanskrit Jābālipura ('City of Sage Jabali'), contemporarily attested in 779 CE by Uddyotana-sūri's Kuvalayamālā.

b_achalgarh.first_mention_attestation: Originally built by the Paramara dynasty and reconstructed, renovated, and named Achalgarh by Maharana Kumbha in 1452 CE.
b_achalgarh.etymology_analysis: Compound of Sanskrit achala ('immovable', referring to Mount Abu / Achaleshwar Mahadev) and Rajasthani gaṛh ('fort'), named when Maharana Kumbha rebuilt the fort in 1452 CE.

b_mandavyapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Māṇḍavyapura (modern Mandore) in the 837 CE Jodhpur inscription of Bauka and the 861 CE Ghantiyala inscription of Kakkuka.
b_mandavyapura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Māṇḍavyapura ('City of Sage Mandavya', modern Mandore), capital of the Mandore Pratiharas, contemporarily attested in the 837 CE Bauka and 861 CE Kakkuka inscriptions.

b_siwana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; bardic tradition attributes Siwana Fort to Vira-narayana, son of 11th-century CE Paramara king Bhoja, and it is historically attested in Alauddin Khalji's 1308 CE siege.
b_siwana.etymology_analysis: Rajasthani hill-fort toponym. Traditionally established in the 11th century CE under the Paramaras; unattested by 867 CE.

b_osian.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the vernacular form Osian by 867 CE; inscriptions of 956 CE (1013 VS) and Jinasena's Harivamsa Purana (783 CE) refer to the town by its earlier Sanskrit name Upakeśapura (Ukeśa).
b_osian.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Rajasthani evolution of Prakrit Ukeśa / Sanskrit Upakeśapura, a major Gurjara-Pratihara religious center. While Upakeśapura is attested by 783 CE, the modern form Osian is post-867.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jinasena's Harivaṃśa Purāṇa (783 CE / Saka 705) and 8th-century Mahavira Jain temple foundation under Vatsaraja.
older_name_by_867.notes: Osian is the later vernacular form of Upakeśapura / Ukeśa.

b_sanderaka.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 10th century CE by Yasobhadra (modern Sanderao in Pali district, Rajasthan).
b_sanderaka.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit/Prakrit toponym Saṇḍeraka (modern Sanderao), founded in the 10th century CE by Yasobhadra and notable as an early Jain center. Unattested by 867 CE.

b_medantaka.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Medantaka (modern Merta City) in the 837 CE Jodhpur stone inscription of Pratihara Bauka (verse 12 calls Medantaka the permanent capital of Nagabhata).
b_medantaka.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Medāntaka (modern Merta), established as capital by Nagabhata of the Mandore Pratiharas and contemporarily attested in the 837 CE Jodhpur inscription of Bauka.

b_purnatallakapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Purnatalla in the 1170 CE (1226 VS) Bijolia rock inscription of the Chahamanas of Shakambhari.
b_purnatallakapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound meaning 'city of the full tank/pond' (from pūrṇa 'full', tallaka 'tank/pond', and pura 'city'). Identified with Purnatalla in the 1170 CE Bijolia inscription (modern Pundlota or Pundla near Merta).

b_naddula.first_mention_attestation: First attested in mid-10th century CE (c. 950 CE) Chahamana records when Lakshmana established the Naddula Chahamana principality.
b_naddula.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized/Prakrit toponym (modern Nadol in Pali district, Rajasthan) derived from naḍa/naḍḍa ('reed, cane') with a diminutive/locative suffix, referring to a reedy or marshy tract.

b_ranakpur.first_mention_attestation: Documented in a 1436 CE copper-plate record and a 1439 CE pillar inscription at the Chaturmukha Jain temple.
b_ranakpur.eponym_details: Named after Rana Kumbha (r. 1433–1468 CE), ruler of Mewar, who patronized the construction of the Ranakpur Jain temple.
b_ranakpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of rāṇaka/Rāṇā (title of Rana Kumbha of Mewar) and Sanskrit pur ('town, settlement'), founded in the late 14th to mid-15th century CE.

b_bhilwara.first_mention_attestation: Earliest extant temple structure (Bada Mandir in Old Bhilwara) dates to the mid-11th century CE (c. 1050 CE).
b_bhilwara.etymology_analysis: Derived either from Bhīl + wāṛā ('settlement/quarter of the Bhil people') or from the local 'Bhiladi' coins minted at the town in the medieval period.

b_chitrakut.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 713 CE Manamori stone inscription at Chittor Fort, naming four Mori (Maurya) rulers of Chitrakuta.
b_chitrakut.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit citra-kūṭa ('variegated/bright peak or fort'), traditionally linked to the 7th-century Mori ruler Chitrangada Mori, later vernacularized as Chittor/Chittorgarh.

b_rampura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE contemporary records; local tradition attributes its foundation to the medieval Bhil chieftain Rama Bhil.
b_rampura.etymology_analysis: Compound of Rāma (attributed in local tradition to Rama Bhil) and Sanskrit pura ('town, settlement').

b_baroli.first_mention_attestation: The Baroli (Badoli) temple complex is dated by art historians to the 10th century CE (c. 900 CE) in the Gurjara-Pratihara style.
b_baroli.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Rajasthani toponym (also spelled Badoli) near Rawatbhata on the Chambal River, likely from baṛ ('banyan') + -olī ('hamlet/row').

b_bhainsrorgarh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval Mewar chronicles around 1330 CE (reign of Rana Hammir), with the present fort built in the 1740s CE.
b_bhainsrorgarh.etymology_analysis: Portmanteau of the names of two caravan traders, Bhainsa Sah and Rora Charan, combined with gaṛh ('fort'), who built the original stronghold to protect caravans.

b_kota.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1264 CE when Prince Jait Singh of Bundi captured Kota and made it a jagir of Bundi.
b_kota.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit koṭa/koṭṭa ('fort, stronghold'), referring to the fortified settlement on the Chambal River established in the 13th–14th century CE.

b_ramgarh.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical or epigraphic records; modern Ramgarh Vishdhari area in Bundi/Baran.
b_ramgarh.etymology_analysis: Compound of Rām (after the Hindu deity Rama or a local ruler) and gaṛh ('fort').

b_bundi.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1241 CE by Rao Deva Singh of the Hada Chauhan clan.
b_bundi.etymology_analysis: Named after Bando Naal, the narrow valley passage between the Aravalli hills where the town is nestled (also traditionally linked to the Meena chieftain Bunda Meena).

b_aghata.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Aghata / Aghatapura (modern Ahar in Udaipur, Rajasthan) in the 953 CE Sarneshwar temple inscription of Guhila ruler Allata and the 977 CE Atpur inscription of Shaktikumara.
b_aghata.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Aghata / Aghatapura (contracted to vernacular Ahar in Udaipur, Rajasthan), the 10th-century CE capital and commercial center of the Guhila dynasty of Mewar.

b_eklingji.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Rana Kumbha's 1460 CE inscription and the 15th-century Ekalinga Mahatmya.
b_eklingji.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit Ekaliṅga ('the single/supreme lingam', an epithet of Shiva) with the honorific suffix -jī.

b_nagahrada.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Nagahrada (modern Nagda) in the 7th century CE (c. 626–646 CE) under Guhila ruler Nagaditya as the first capital of Mewar.
b_nagahrada.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Nāgahrada ('serpent lake', or lake of Nagaditya), the early capital of the Guhilas of Mewar, later contracted to Nagda.

b_jagadamba.first_mention_attestation: Earliest inscription at the Ambika Mata (Jagadamba) temple in Jagat is dated 961 CE, recording repairs to the shrine.
b_jagadamba.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Jagadambā ('Mother of the World', an epithet of Durga/Ambika Devi), referring to the 10th-century Ambika Mata temple at Jagat.

b_rishabhdeo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE contemporary records; medieval Jain pilgrimage center (Kesariyaji) in Udaipur district.
b_rishabhdeo.etymology_analysis: Named after Lord Rishabhadeva (Rishabhanatha), the first Jain Tirthankara, enshrined at the Kesariyaji temple.

b_nagauda.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 12th-century CE sources (c. 1121 CE Chahamana/Ghaznavid records of Nagaur Fort), while earlier Chahamana records use Ahichchhatrapura or Nagapura.
b_nagauda.etymology_analysis: Vernacularized from Sanskrit Nāgapura / Nāgadurga ('city/fortress of the Nagas'), yielding medieval Nagauda/Nagaur.

b_ladnu.first_mention_attestation: Established as a Jain center in the 10th century CE, with the earliest dated architectural/epigraphic remains (Shantinatha temple torana) from 1079 CE.
b_ladnu.etymology_analysis: Rajasthani toponym (also spelled Ladnun) in Didwana-Kuchaman district, historically known as Chanderi Nagari.

b_makrana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE records; marble quarry town prominent from the Mughal period (17th century CE); currently unoccupied in repo.
b_makrana.etymology_analysis: Traditionally linked to artisans from Makran or Persian muqarnas; unoccupied holding in current repo state.

b_kuchaman.first_mention_attestation: Kuchaman Fort is traditionally dated to the 9th–10th century CE (c. 950 CE Pratihara-Chauhan era), with no pre-867 CE contemporary inscription.
b_kuchaman.etymology_analysis: Rajasthani toponym associated with the medieval hill fort overlooking Kuchaman City.

b_aror.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 711–712 CE Arabic accounts (al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan) as al-Rur/Aror, capital of Sindh captured by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim.
b_aror.etymology_analysis: Medieval Sindhi/Arabic name (Aror/Alor) evolved from ancient Roruka, the capital of the Sauvira kingdom.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Early Buddhist literature (c. 4th–3rd century BCE) as capital of Sauvira.
older_name_by_867.notes: Aror is identified with ancient Roruka, capital of Sauvira.

b_siraj_ji_takri.first_mention_attestation: Modern Sindhi name for a 5th–6th century CE Buddhist archaeological site in Khairpur District; ancient name unattested.
b_siraj_ji_takri.etymology_analysis: Modern Sindhi toponym meaning 'Hillock of Siraj', applied to the ruins of a 5th–6th century CE Buddhist settlement on the Rohri Hills.

b_bhakkar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval Persian chronicles of Sindh such as the Chach Nama (c. 1216 CE) as the Indus island fortress of Bakhar/Bukkur.
b_bhakkar.etymology_analysis: Sindhi name (also spelled Bukkur) for the fortified island on the Indus River between Rohri and Sukkur.

b_shikarpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1677 CE as a hunting ground of the Mahar tribe in northern Sindh.
b_shikarpur.etymology_analysis: Persian-Indo-Aryan hybrid compound meaning 'hunting town' (from Persian shikār 'hunt' + Sanskrit/Sindhi pūr 'town').

b_larkana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE records; modern city developed from the 18th century CE (formerly Chandka).
b_larkana.etymology_analysis: Sindhi toponym (Lāṛkāṇo) derived from the Larik tribe who settled in the region, replacing the older regional name Chandka.

b_mohenjo_daro.first_mention_attestation: Modern Sindhi name recorded during archaeological excavations in the 1920s (1922 CE); the Bronze Age (c. 2500 BCE) city's original name is unknown.
b_mohenjo_daro.etymology_analysis: Modern Sindhi name meaning 'Mound of the Dead', applied to the ruined Indus Valley Civilization metropolis.

b_rajanpur.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1732–1733 CE by Makhdum Sheikh Rajan Shah of Sitpur after he captured the estates from the Nahar rulers in southern Punjab, Pakistan.
b_rajanpur.eponym_details: Named after Makhdum Sheikh Rajan Shah of Sitpur, who founded the town in 1732–1733 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name Makhdum Sheikh Rajan Shah

b_rajanpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of the founder's personal name Rajan (Makhdum Sheikh Rajan Shah) and the Indo-Aryan settlement suffix -pur ('town'), founded in 1732–1733 CE.

b_rojhan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1834 CE historical records as the Mazari Baloch stronghold during Sikh-Mazari conflicts.
b_rojhan.etymology_analysis: Local Balochi/Saraiki toponym for the Mazari tribal headquarters in Rajanpur District.

b_dajal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical records; town in Rajanpur District, Punjab.
b_dajal.etymology_analysis: Local Saraiki/Punjabi toponym in Rajanpur District, also lending its name to the Dajal cattle breed.

b_badah.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical records; modern town in Larkana District, Sindh.
b_badah.etymology_analysis: Modern Sindhi toponym in Larkana District, Sindh.

b_sibi.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 10th-century CE Arab geographers Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi as Siwi/Sibi, capital of Balis (Walishtan).
b_sibi.etymology_analysis: Derived from medieval Siwi/Sibi, traditionally linked to the pre-Islamic Sewa dynasty of Balochistan.

b_pul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical records; minor locality in Sibi District, Balochistan.
b_pul.etymology_analysis: Persian/Indo-Aryan pul ('bridge'), referring to a river crossing in Sibi District.

b_asfanjay.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Isfanjay/Asfanjay by 10th-century CE Arab geographers Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi in the province of Balis.
b_asfanjay.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic/Persian toponym (Isfanjay) recorded in 10th-century Islamic geographical works for a town in Balis/Sibi.

b_mastang.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 10th-century CE Arab geographers Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi as a town in Balis (Walishtan).
b_mastang.etymology_analysis: Balochi/Brahui toponym (modern Mastung) attested in 10th-century Arabic geographical texts.

b_shal.first_mention_attestation: Earliest historical references to the Quetta/Shal valley date to the 11th century CE (c. 1020s CE) during Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns.
b_shal.etymology_analysis: Traditional name (Shal / Shalkot) of the Quetta valley and settlement, later superseded by Pashto kwatta ('fort', Quetta).

b_debul.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 711–712 CE Arabic accounts (al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan) as the port city conquered by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, corroborated by 727 CE Kufic inscriptions at Banbhore.
b_debul.etymology_analysis: Arabicized (Daybul/Debul) from Sanskrit/Prakrit devālaya/deval ('temple'), referring to the prominent coastal temple port of Sindh.

b_thatta.first_mention_attestation: Construction of Thatta as the Samma capital was ordered by Jam Nizamuddin II in 1495 CE (with Makli Necropolis tombs beginning in the 14th century CE).
b_thatta.etymology_analysis: Sindhi toponym (Ṭhaṭṭo) referring to the alluvial bank/settlement in the lower Indus delta.

b_shahbandar.first_mention_attestation: Prominent Kalhora-era port town in Sindh where the British East India Company established a trading factory in 1758 CE.
b_shahbandar.etymology_analysis: Persian compound meaning 'royal port' or 'harbormaster' (shāh 'king' + bandar 'port').

b_nirun.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 711 CE Arabic accounts (al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan) as al-Nirun, which surrendered peacefully to Muhammad ibn al-Qasim.
b_nirun.etymology_analysis: Early medieval Sindhi toponym (Nirun / Nerunkot) recorded in Arabic conquest histories, located at or near modern Hyderabad, Sindh.

b_kolachi.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 18th-century records (1742 CE Dutch document as Karachee; local legend places Mai Kolachi in the 11th century CE).
b_kolachi.eponym_details: Named after Mai Kolachi, a legendary 11th-century CE fisherwoman who settled near the Indus delta during the Soomra dynasty.
b_kolachi.etymology_analysis: Named after the legendary 11th-century fisherwoman Mai Kolachi (or the Kolachi/Kulachi tribe), which evolved into modern Karachi.

b_mansura.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 738 CE by Umayyad commanders (Amr ibn Muhammad or Mansur ibn Jamhur) and attested in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan and 8th-century Sindh coinage.
b_mansura.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Manṣūra ('the victorious'), founded as the Umayyad capital of Sindh near the earlier cities of al-Mahfuza and Brahmanabad.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (712 CE conquest of Brahmanabad; c. 730 CE founding of al-Mahfuza).
older_name_by_867.notes: Mansura was founded immediately adjacent to Brahmanabad and al-Mahfuza.

b_mirpur_khas.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1806 CE by Mir Ali Murad Talpur of the Mankani Talpur dynasty.
b_mirpur_khas.eponym_details: Named after its founder Mir Ali Murad Talpur (1806 CE), with 'Mir' as the Talpur royal title.
b_mirpur_khas.etymology_analysis: Compound of Mīr ('prince/chief', after Mir Ali Murad Talpur), pur ('town'), and khāṣ ('special/royal').

b_matiari.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical records; medieval settlement in central Sindh.
b_matiari.etymology_analysis: Traditional Sindhi etymology derives Matiari from Mut Waree ('place where water pots are kept').

b_nasarpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources (late 18th-century Tuhfat al-Kiram and local tradition attribute it to 750 CE / 132 AH).
b_nasarpur.etymology_analysis: Compound of Arabic Naṣr (attributed in late Sindhi tradition to Nasr bin Muhammad al-Khuzai) and pur ('town').

b_ranikot.first_mention_attestation: Ranikot Fort in Jamshoro district, Sindh, Pakistan was constructed or extensively rebuilt in its present monumental form c. 1812 CE under the Talpur Mirs (with earlier fortification phases attributed by archaeologists to the 17th century CE); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

morphemes.translation: queen (also associated with the Rani Nai seasonal stream)

b_ranikot.etymology_analysis: Sindhi compound Ranikot ('Queen's Fort' or 'Fort on the Rani Nai stream'), referring to the massive Talpur-era hill fortress in the Kirthar Range of Sindh.

b_sharusan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 711 CE Arabic conquest accounts (al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan) as Sadusan/Sharusan (modern Sehwan).
b_sharusan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic/Persian geographical name (Sadūsān / Sharūsān) for Sehwan, derived from Sindhu-vān / Siwistān.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek accounts of Alexander the Great's campaign (326 BCE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Sehwan/Sharusan is identified with ancient Sindomana, capital of King Sambos.

b_khudabad.first_mention_attestation: Established as the capital of the Kalhora dynasty of Sindh c. 1700–1701 CE by Mian Yar Muhammad Kalhoro in modern Dadu district, Sindh, Pakistan.
b_khudabad.etymology_analysis: Persian compound Khudabad ('City of God'), founded c. 1700–1701 CE by Mian Yar Muhammad Kalhoro as the capital of Kalhora Sindh.

b_siwistan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 711 CE Arabic conquest accounts (al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan) as Siwistan/Sadusan (modern Sehwan).
b_siwistan.etymology_analysis: Persianized toponym (Siwistān) for Sehwan, derived from Sivi/Sindhu-vān + -stān ('land of').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek accounts of Alexander the Great's campaign (326 BCE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Siwistan (Sehwan) is identified with ancient Sindomana, capital of King Sambos.

b_mir_rukan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; modern village name associated with the 6th–11th century CE Thul Mir Rukan Buddhist stupa.
b_mir_rukan.etymology_analysis: Modern Sindhi village name ('Mir Rukan') applied to the archaeological site of the Thul Mir Rukan Buddhist stupa.

b_sonda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical records; village and Chaukhandi-style necropolis near Thatta in lower Sindh.
b_sonda.etymology_analysis: Sindhi toponym for a settlement and historic graveyard near Thatta in lower Sindh.

b_amarkot.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally founded in the 11th century CE (c. 1050 CE) as the desert fortress of Amarkot / Umerkot in Sindh, Pakistan (associated with Sodha Rajput ruler Rana Amar Singh or Soomra ruler Umer Soomro), and prominently documented in Mughal chronicles as the 1542 CE birthplace of Emperor Akbar.
b_amarkot.eponym_details: Named after either Rana Amar Singh (11th-century Sodha Rajput founder of Amarkot) or Umer Soomro (medieval Soomra ruler of Sindh, giving the variant Umerkot).

morphemes.translation: personal name Rana Amar Singh (or Sindhi Umer Soomro)

b_amarkot.etymology_analysis: Compound of the personal name Amar (Rana Amar Singh; variant Umer after Umer Soomro) and kot ('fort'), denoting the historic Thar desert stronghold of Umerkot in Sindh.

b_badin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical records; town in lower Sindh prominent from the Samma/Mughal period.
b_badin.etymology_analysis: Sindhi toponym for the main town of Badin District in lower Sindh.

b_karoonjar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; granite mountain range near Nagarparkar in Tharparkar, Sindh.
b_karoonjar.etymology_analysis: Sindhi oronym for the 19-km granite hill range in Nagarparkar on the edge of the Rann of Kutch.

b_ludrava.first_mention_attestation: First firmly attested in 1025 CE when Mahmud of Ghazni besieged Lodhruva (though Bhati tradition places its founding in the 8th–9th century CE).
b_ludrava.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized/Rajasthani toponym (Lodrava/Lodhruva), the medieval desert capital of the Bhati Rajputs prior to Jaisalmer.

b_jaisalmer.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1156 CE by Bhati Rajput ruler Rawal Jaisal on Trikuta Hill in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan, relocating the Bhati capital from Lodhruva.
b_jaisalmer.eponym_details: Named after Rawal Jaisal, the Bhati Rajput chief who founded the city and hill fort in 1156 CE.
b_jaisalmer.etymology_analysis: Compound of the founder's personal name Jaisal (Rawal Jaisal) and mer (from Sanskrit Meru, 'hill/mountain'), meaning 'Hill Fort of Jaisal', founded in 1156 CE.

b_phalavardhika.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Sanskritized name of Phalodi, whose earliest dated temple/epigraphic records begin around 1230 CE (Kalyan Raoji temple).
b_phalavardhika.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Phalavardhikā ('fruit-increasing/prosperous'), the historical Sanskritized form of modern Phalodi in western Rajasthan.

b_juna_barmer.first_mention_attestation: Old Barmer (Bahadmer), founded in the 12th–13th century CE (c. 1200 CE) before the settlement shifted to modern Barmer.
b_juna_barmer.etymology_analysis: Rajasthani jūnā ('old') + Bāhaḍmer ('hill-fort of Bahada'), referring to the older medieval site of Barmer.

b_satyapura.first_mention_attestation: Historical Sanskrit name of Sanchore, epigraphically attested from at least Chaulukya king Mularaja I's 995 CE Balera/Satyapura copper-plate grant (and later in 14th-century chronicles of Alauddin Khalji's 1311 CE raid).
b_satyapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Satyapura ('city of truth'), which evolved phonetically into modern Sanchore in Jalore district, Rajasthan.

b_kiratakupa.first_mention_attestation: Original Sanskrit name of Kiradu; temple construction dates to the 10th–11th century CE (Someshvara temple c. 1020 CE) with inscriptions from 1152 CE and 1178 CE.
b_kiratakupa.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Kirātakūpa ('well of the Kiratas'), which contracted to modern Kiradu in Barmer district, Rajasthan.

b_kasara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kasahrada (Kayadra) in the 1178 CE Battle of Kasahrada and the Sundha Hill inscription.
b_kasara.etymology_analysis: Vernacularized from Sanskrit Kāsahrada ('lake of kasa grass'), a strategic pass near Mount Abu in southern Rajasthan.

b_vijnot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; archaeological mound in Ghotki District, Sindh containing Kushan-era (2nd–3rd century CE) remains.
b_vijnot.etymology_analysis: Sindhi name (Vijnot / Vinjrot) for an ancient ruined city mound along the Rainee River in Ghotki District.

b_ghotki.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1447 CE by Pir Mohsin Shah according to Sindhi historian Mirza Kalich Beg.
b_ghotki.etymology_analysis: Sindhi toponym associated with the Ghoto tribe in northern Sindh, founded in the mid-15th century CE.

b_bhatiya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1004 CE during Mahmud of Ghazni's Siege of Bhatiya, narrated by al-Utbi and al-Biruni.
b_bhatiya.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bhati Rajput rulers of the fortified principality recorded by Ghaznavid historians between Narayan and Rohri.
